daily_entries.summary: The Iran war ran a fifth straight day off the kinetic register, on the ceremonial and diplomatic track. Following the July 6 main Tehran procession — which Tehran's mayor had projected at up to 20 million and which unfolded as one of the largest gatherings in the city's history — the funeral cortege for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei moved on July 7 to Qom, with prayers at the Jamkaran mosque and the Fatima Masoumeh shrine. The rites are due to reach Najaf and Karbala in Iraq on July 8 (an official reception with Iraq's prime minister at the Imam Ali shrine) and conclude with burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad — Khamenei's birthplace — on July 9. The newly named Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei (designated March 9), had still not appeared publicly; reporting now ties his months-long absence both to an Israeli threat to assassinate Iran's new leader and to injuries sustained in the Feb 28 decapitation strike (US officials in March had said he was 'wounded and likely disfigured,' and later reports described severe facial and leg injuries) — leaving the succession/who-runs-Iran question open. US-Iran talks stayed paused for the funeral week; Qatar said the earlier Doha round made 'positive progress' with no breakthrough and that further discussions would be scheduled 'at the earliest possible time' after the rites. Oil markets held Brent near the pre-war ~$72/bbl, with Saudi exports ~90% of the pre-war baseline, UAE exports above 3.9M bpd, and total Hormuz flows above 10M bpd. The Hormuz-governance dispute stayed unresolved — Iran maintaining mid-August 'service fees' the US rejects, and the UK and France backing an Oman-led freedom-of-navigation effort. The ground-invasion rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory: no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stays lifted (Day 19). No new strikes or shipping incidents were reported.
details: FUNERAL RITES MOVE TO QOM (July 7, 2026): After the July 6 main Tehran procession (Imam Hossein Square to Azadi Square, projected up to 20 million mourners), the cortege for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei reached Qom on July 7 for prayers at the Jamkaran mosque and the Fatima Masoumeh shrine. The six-day schedule continues to Najaf and Karbala, Iraq (July 8, Imam Ali shrine, reception with Iraq's PM) and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad on July 9. (CNN/Al Jazeera funeral coverage, July 3-6, 2026; Wikipedia, 'State funeral of Ali Khamenei,' July 2026.)

SUCCESSION QUESTION STAYS LIVE — NEW SUPREME LEADER STILL ABSENT (July 6-7, 2026): New Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, named to succeed his father on March 9, had still not appeared publicly. Reporting attributed his absence both to security concerns after an Israeli threat to assassinate Iran's new leader and to injuries from the Feb 28 opening strike — Defense Secretary Hegseth said in March he was 'wounded and likely disfigured,' and later reports described severe facial and leg injuries (possible loss of a leg). Three of Khamenei's other sons had prayed at the coffin on July 5; the designated successor did not appear. (CNBC; TIME; US News; The Tribune, July 5, 2026.)

US-IRAN TALKS REMAIN PAUSED FOR FUNERAL WEEK (July 6-7, 2026): The indirect US-Iran track, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, stayed paused for the funeral; Qatar said the earlier Doha round made 'positive progress' with no breakthrough and that further discussions would be scheduled 'at the earliest possible time' after the rites. Core disputes remained open — the US rejects any Iranian-led Hormuz toll mechanism, no frozen funds have moved, and the IAEA-access dispute over the US-bombed Fordow/Natanz/Isfahan sites is unresolved (Speaker Ghalibaf again denied access to the bombed sites). (Al Jazeera; CBS News; CNN, July 1-6, 2026.)

HORMUZ / OIL — DISPUTE UNRESOLVED, PRICES NEAR PRE-WAR (July 6-7, 2026): Iran maintained it would charge transit 'service fees' once the 60-day toll-free window ends around mid-August (with 'special treatment' for 'friendly' nations), a mechanism the US rejects, while the UK and France pledged to help Oman keep navigation free. Brent held near the pre-war ~$72/bbl after OPEC+ agreed July 5 to raise August output by 188,000 bpd; Saudi crude exports ran ~90% of the pre-war baseline, UAE exports topped 3.9M bpd, and total Hormuz flows stayed above 10M bpd. No new strikes or shipping incidents were reported July 6-7. (TradingEconomics/CNBC; RFE/RL; CBS News, July 1-6, 2026.)

HORMUZ-AFFECTED ECONOMIES (early July 2026): The war's supply shock kept straining import-dependent economies even as flows recovered: Slovenia became the first EU country to impose fuel rationing (50L/day private), Bangladesh rationed fuel and shortened university terms, India managed an LPG squeeze (spring arrivals down 40%+) while lifting record discounted Russian crude, and Japan and South Korea — ranked most exposed by petrochemical dependence — kept up non-Gulf sourcing (Seoul's energy minister said it faced no supply problem for over a year). (Zero Carbon Analytics; Oxford Energy; Reuters, July 2026.)

alternate_readings.reading: Mojtaba Khamenei's continued public absence through the Qom leg admits the same two readings tracked since July 5, now sharpened by reporting on injuries. One treats the absence as the sum of wartime security prudence (an Israeli threat to kill Iran's new leader) and genuine incapacity from the Feb 28 strike that US officials said left him 'wounded and likely disfigured' — with authority still exercised through the SNSC and IRGC as designed. The other treats the months-long non-appearance since his March 9 designation as evidence of a leadership vacuum: that Mojtaba may be too incapacitated to govern or is a figurehead, and that the security establishment is effectively running Iran, which would bear on who can actually deliver on any US-Iran deal.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings rest on the same on-record facts: Mojtaba was named successor March 9; he has not appeared publicly since; his other brothers prayed at the coffin July 5 while he did not; US officials said in March he was 'wounded and likely disfigured' and later reports described severe facial/leg injuries; and Israel renewed a threat against Iran's new leader. Which reading is correct depends on non-public information about the severity of his injuries, his current health, and his real decision-making role, none of it determinable from open sources today.
public_assertion_by: CNBC / TIME / US News (July 5, 2026): the new supreme leader is absent from the funeral; reporting cites both an assassination threat and strike injuries.
US officials (Hegseth, March 2026): Mojtaba was 'wounded and likely disfigured' in the Feb 28 strike.
Iran-watchers and analysts: cite the non-appearance as a marker of possible IRGC ascendancy or a contested/hollow succession.

alternate_readings.why_unresolvable: Resolution requires non-public knowledge of Mojtaba Khamenei's injuries, health, location, and real authority; open sources currently show only his continued public absence, consistent with both prudent concealment/recovery and genuine incapacity.

daily_entries.headline: RUSSIA-UKRAINE — JULY 6-7: UKRAINE STRIKES OMSK — RUSSIA'S LARGEST REFINERY, ~2,500-3,000 KM AWAY, THE DEEPEST STRIKE OF THE WAR (ALSO YAROSLAVL/SLAVNEFT-YANOS AND UST-LUGA). RUSSIA ANSWERED WITH A MASS OVERNIGHT BARRAGE ON KYIV (351 DRONES + 68 MISSILES) THAT KILLED ~22 AND INJURED ~90 NATIONWIDE. TRUMP HELD A ~90-MIN CALL WITH PUTIN ('BUSINESSLIKE AND VERY CONSTRUCTIVE') AND SPOKE WITH ZELENSKY AHEAD OF THE NATO SUMMIT IN ANKARA (JULY 7-8), WHERE HE IS SET TO MEET ZELENSKY AND GERMANY IS FINANCING TWO PATRIOT SYSTEMS. KOSTIANTYNIVKA STAYS CONTESTED — RUSSIA PROPOSED A LOCAL CEASEFIRE (UKRAINE REJECTED IT), AND ISW PUTS RUSSIAN PRESENCE AT ~37% OF THE CITY (~4.3% OF LYMAN), CALLING PUTIN'S 96% CLAIM 'GREATLY EXAGGERATED.' RUSSIA HOLDS ~20% WITH NO CONFIRMED NET CHANGE. NO US GROUND-DEPLOYMENT SURGE.
daily_entries.summary: The Russia-Ukraine war stayed on its established July track — a deep-strike energy war, mass Russian barrages on cities, contested Donbas ground claims, and stalled diplomacy — while high-level contacts picked up ahead of a NATO summit. On July 6 Ukrainian long-range drones struck the Omsk refinery in Siberia — Russia's largest, some 2,500-3,000 km from Ukraine — described as the deepest strike into Russia of the full-scale war and, per Ukraine's General Staff, the last of Russia's eleven largest gasoline-producing refineries to be hit; the same wave hit the Slavneft-Yanos refinery at Yaroslavl and Novatek's Ust-Luga Baltic complex. Overnight into July 6 Russia launched a mass barrage — about 351 drones and 68 missiles, mainly at Kyiv (all 29 ballistic missiles reportedly striking targets) — that Zelensky said killed about 22 and injured roughly 90 nationwide (15 killed and 58 injured in Kyiv city, plus 8 killed in Kyiv region), framed by Moscow as retaliation for Ukraine's refinery campaign. Over the weekend Trump held a roughly 90-minute call with Putin (the Kremlin called it 'businesslike and very constructive') and separately spoke with Zelensky, who said 'there is a real prospect to put an end to this war' and agreed to continue talks at the NATO summit in Ankara (July 7-8), where Trump was set to meet him; Germany signalled it would finance two Patriot systems for Ukraine amid a PAC-3 interceptor shortage worsened by Middle East demand. On the ground, Kostiantynivka stayed contested — Russia proposed a local ceasefire (paired with a body handover) that Ukraine rejected, and ISW put Russian presence at about 37% of the city and 4.3% of Lyman, calling Putin's claim of 96% control 'greatly exaggerated.' Russia holds about 20% of Ukraine with no confirmed net change, and there was no US ground-deployment surge.
details: OMSK — DEEPEST STRIKE OF THE WAR (July 6, 2026): Ukrainian long-range drones struck the Omsk refinery, Russia's largest (~8.4M t/yr ELOU-AVT-11 unit), some 2,500-3,000 km from Ukraine — described as the deepest strike into Russia of the full-scale war and, per Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, the last of Russia's eleven biggest gasoline-producing refineries to be targeted. The same wave hit the Slavneft-Yanos refinery at Yaroslavl (~700 km) and Novatek's Ust-Luga Baltic complex. Ukraine has struck Russian refineries nearly 200 times in H1 2026. (United24; Moscow Times; Ukrainska Pravda; Euronews, July 6, 2026.)

RUSSIA'S MASS BARRAGE ON KYIV (overnight into July 6, 2026): Russia launched ~351 drones and 68 missiles, concentrated on Kyiv (all 29 ballistic missiles reportedly hit their targets); Zelensky's evening address cited ~22 killed and ~90 injured nationwide, with 15 killed and 58 injured in Kyiv city and 8 killed in Kyiv region. Podilskyi district was hit hardest; residential high-rises were struck. Moscow framed it as retaliation for Ukraine's long-range strikes. (NPR; NBC News; CNN; Ukrinform, July 6, 2026.)

TRUMP-PUTIN AND TRUMP-ZELENSKY CALLS; NATO SUMMIT IN ANKARA (July 4-7, 2026): Trump held a ~90-minute call with Putin (Kremlin: 'businesslike and very constructive'; Trump offered to help find a solution) and separately spoke with Zelensky, who said there was 'a real prospect to put an end to this war' and agreed to continue talks at the NATO summit of 32 heads of state in Ankara (July 7-8), where Trump was scheduled to meet him. The core impasse held — Russia insists on full control of Donbas; Ukraine rejects it. (NBC News; CNBC; NPR; The Hill, July 4-6, 2026.)

PATRIOTS / AIR DEFENSE (July 6-7, 2026): Under Trump's arrangement (US supplies systems, NATO nations pay), Germany signalled willingness to finance two Patriot systems for Ukraine, with a 100-interceptor coalition schedule and a Germany-Ukraine barter deal pending into the summit; German Defense Minister Pistorius said Germany had no remaining launcher capacity. A PAC-3 MSE interceptor shortage — worsened by Middle East demand (Israel, Saudi, UAE, Qatar) — constrains supply as Ukraine leans on Patriots for ballistic intercepts. (TWZ; Defence Ukraine; NPR, July 6-7, 2026.)

KOSTIANTYNIVKA STAYS CONTESTED (July 4-6, 2026): Russia proposed a local ceasefire in Kostiantynivka paired with a handover of bodies; Russia said Ukraine rejected it. ISW mapping put Russian presence at ~37% of the city and only ~4.3% of Lyman, calling Putin's claim of 96% control of Kostiantynivka 'greatly exaggerated' and characterizing gains as small-group infiltration (~50 m/day) rather than consolidated control. Russia holds ~20% of Ukraine with no confirmed net change. (Ukrainska Pravda; Al Jazeera; ISW/Russia Matters; Euromaidan Press, July 4-5, 2026.)

The contested Kostiantynivka claim is tracked as an open question (kostiantynivka-control-contested-july-2026).

alternate_readings.reading: Russia's claim to control Kostiantynivka still reads two ways from the same record. Moscow's reading (Putin's ~96%-control claim, Gerasimov's July 3 'liberation' report, state media) treats the city as captured or nearly so — a milestone in the Spring-Summer 2026 offensive, reinforced by Russia's offer of a 'local ceasefire' as the magnanimous victor. Ukraine's reading (General Staff, Zelensky, front commanders) treats the Russian presence as small-group infiltration being cleared, holds that the city remains under Ukrainian control, and reads the local-ceasefire offer as a propaganda device Kyiv rejected. ISW sides closer to Ukraine — ~37% Russian presence, Putin's 96% 'greatly exaggerated' — but granular street-level control is not verifiable from open sources in real time.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings cite the same documented facts: Putin's/Gerasimov's control claims; Russia's local-ceasefire-plus-body-handover offer and its account that Ukraine rejected it; Ukraine's denial that the city has fallen; and ISW's ~37%-of-city / ~4.3%-of-Lyman mapping calling the Russian claims exaggerated. Which side holds which blocks of Kostiantynivka cannot be adjudicated from open sources today.
public_assertion_by: Russian side: Putin's ~96%-control claim, Gerasimov's July 3 'liberation' report, and the local-ceasefire offer imply effective control.
Ukrainian side: General Staff and Zelensky say the city remains contested/held and rejected the local ceasefire.

alternate_readings.why_unresolvable: Real-time, street-level control of a contested frontline city cannot be confirmed from open sources; both sides' claims are self-reported and the independent trackers explicitly caveat their assessments.

daily_entries.headline: DAY 130 — CEASEFIRE DAY 90 / US BLOCKADE LIFTED DAY 18 — MAIN FUNERAL DAY IN TEHRAN: THE CENTRAL PROCESSION FOR SLAIN SUPREME LEADER AYATOLLAH ALI KHAMENEI STEPPED OFF AT 6 A.M. LOCAL ON A ~10 KM ROUTE FROM IMAM HOSSEIN SQUARE TO AZADI SQUARE, WITH TEHRAN'S MAYOR PROJECTING UP TO 20 MILLION MOURNERS — POTENTIALLY THE LARGEST GATHERING IN THE CITY'S HISTORY. THE RITES CONTINUE TO QOM (JAMKARAN, JULY 7), NAJAF (JULY 8, IRAQI PM RECEPTION AT THE IMAM ALI SHRINE) AND BURIAL AT THE IMAM REZA SHRINE IN MASHHAD (JULY 9). NEW SUPREME LEADER MOJTABA KHAMENEI (NAMED MARCH 9) STILL HAD NOT APPEARED PUBLICLY, KEEPING THE SUCCESSION / WHO-RUNS-IRAN QUESTION LIVE. US-IRAN TALKS REMAINED PAUSED FOR THE FUNERAL WEEK (TO RESUME 'AT THE EARLIEST POSSIBLE TIME' AFTER, PER QATAR). ON HORMUZ, IRAN'S AMBASSADOR TO CHINA REAFFIRMED TRANSIT 'SERVICE FEES' ONCE THE 60-DAY PAUSE ENDS (MID-AUGUST), WITH 'SPECIAL TREATMENT' FOR FRIENDLY NATIONS — AN IDEA THE US REJECTS — WHILE IRAN WARNED AGAINST ANY 'MILITARY DISPLAY OF EXTRA-REGIONAL POWERS' AND THE UK/FRANCE BACKED OMAN ON FREE NAVIGATION. OPEC+ AGREED JULY 5 TO RAISE AUGUST OUTPUT BY 188,000 BPD; OIL MARKETS REOPENED JULY 6 AFTER THE US HOLIDAY WEEKEND WITH BRENT NEAR ITS PRE-WAR ~$72/BBL (SAUDI EXPORTS ~90% OF PRE-WAR, UAE >3.9M BPD, TOTAL HORMUZ FLOWS >10M BPD). THE GROUND RUNG STAYED UNCHANGED AND DE-ESCALATORY ON THE US SIDE — NO US TROOPS IN IRAN, NO KHARG ASSAULT, NO NEW ARG/MEU ORDER, NO DRAFT; BLOCKADE STILL LIFTED (DAY 18). ISRAEL RENEWED A THREAT TO KILL IRAN'S NEW SUPREME LEADER. NO NEW STRIKES OR SHIPPING INCIDENTS REPORTED JULY 5-6.
daily_entries.summary: The Iran war again ran on the ceremonial and diplomatic register, not the ground one, as July 6 brought the central and largest day of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's six-day state funeral. The main Tehran procession stepped off at 6 a.m. local along a roughly 10-kilometre route from Imam Hossein Square to Azadi Square; Tehran's mayor said attendance could reach 20 million, which would make it the largest gathering in the city's history and the largest state funeral in Iran's, exceeding Khomeini's 1989 rites. The cortege is due to reach Qom (Jamkaran) on July 7, Najaf in Iraq on July 8 (an official reception with Iraq's prime minister at the Imam Ali shrine), and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad — Khamenei's birthplace — on July 9. The newly named Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei (designated March 9), had still not appeared publicly, leaving the succession/who-runs-Iran question open. US-Iran talks stayed paused for the funeral week, with Qatar saying the indirect track made 'positive progress' and further discussions would be scheduled 'at the earliest possible time' afterward. On the Strait, Iran's ambassador to China reaffirmed that transit 'service fees' would apply once the 60-day toll-free window ends around mid-August, promising 'special treatment' for 'friendly' nations — a mechanism the US rejects — while Iran warned against any 'military display of extra-regional powers' in the Strait and the UK and France pledged to help Oman keep navigation free. On energy, OPEC+ agreed on July 5 to raise August output by 188,000 bpd; US oil markets reopened July 6 after the Independence Day weekend with Brent near its pre-war ~$72/bbl, Saudi crude exports back to ~90% of the pre-war baseline, UAE exports above 3.9M bpd, and total Hormuz flows back above 10M bpd. The ground-invasion rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stays lifted (Day 18). Israel renewed a threat to kill Iran's new supreme leader. No new strikes or shipping incidents were reported on July 5-6.

The schedule runs to Qom (Jamkaran mosque, prayers July 7), Najaf, Iraq (July 8, Imam Ali shrine, reception with Iraq's PM and senior officials), and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad on July 9. daily_entries.headline: RUSSIA-UKRAINE — JULY 5-6: KOSTIANTYNIVKA CONTROL STILL CONTESTED; DEEP-STRIKE WAR CONTINUES. UKRAINE KEPT UP ITS REFINERY CAMPAIGN (LUKOIL-NIZHEGORODORGSINTEZ, RUSSIA'S 4TH-LARGEST, HALTED AFTER A JULY 2 STRIKE; UFA HIT TWICE IN A WEEK; ST. PETERSBURG OIL TERMINAL / KRONSTADT JULY 4). RUSSIA PRESSED MASS STRIKES ON KYIV (THE JULY 1-2 BARRAGE KILLED AT LEAST 17-31). ZELENSKY, AFTER A ~40-MIN JULY 4 CALL WITH TRUMP, PRESSED ALLIES TO ACCELERATE PATRIOT DELIVERIES AND WARNED OF ANOTHER LARGE-SCALE RUSSIAN ATTACK. daily_entries.summary: The Russia-Ukraine war stayed on its established July track — contested Donbas ground claims, a deep-strike energy war, and stalled diplomacy. Russia's July 3 claim (Gerasimov to Putin) that its forces had 'liberated' Kostiantynivka remained disputed: Ukraine's 19th Army Corps commander Yuriy 'Madyar' Butusov reported his troops pushing Russian infiltrators back out of the city at a loss ratio of about three Ukrainians to 53 Russians, and ISW and DeepState continued to characterize the fighting as small-group infiltration rather than consolidated control (DeepState logged only ~12 square miles of net Russian gain over the four weeks to June 23, underscoring that 2024-25 momentum has largely stalled). Ukraine kept striking Russia's oil sector — the Lukoil-Nizhegorodorgsintez refinery (Russia's fourth-largest, second-largest gasoline producer) halted after a July 2 drone strike, Ufa was hit twice in a week, and the St. Petersburg oil terminal and Kronstadt were struck July 4. Russia pressed mass strikes on Kyiv (the July 1-2 barrage killed at least 17, with earlier tallies up to 31). After a roughly 40-minute July 4 call with Trump that agreed to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and expand joint drone/weapons production, Zelensky pressed allies to accelerate Patriot deliveries and warned Russia was preparing another large-scale attack. Peace talks stayed stalled, with Putin still insisting on the 2022 Istanbul Protocols; Russia holds about 20% of Ukraine with no confirmed net change, and there was no US ground-deployment surge.

daily_entries.summary: The Iran war ran entirely on the ceremonial and diplomatic register through July 4-5, not the ground one. Iran's six-day state funeral for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei — killed in the Feb 28 US-Israeli opening strike and buried only now after repeated wartime postponement — continued into its second day: the coffin lay in state at Tehran's Grand Mosalla with mourners chanting 'revenge' and 'death to America' in roughly 100°F heat (authorities sprayed vaporized water on the crowds), ahead of July 5 funeral prayers and a procession in Qom (Fatima Masoumeh shrine and Jamkaran mosque), with the cortege due to reach Najaf and Karbala in Iraq on July 8 and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad on July 9. Officials project 15-20 million mourners over the week, which would make it the largest state funeral in Iranian history, exceeding Khomeini's 1989 rites; delegations from more than 70 countries attended, including Russia (former president Dmitry Medvedev as Putin's special emissary), Pakistan (PM Shehbaz Sharif), Iraq's president and prime minister, the Afghan Taliban foreign minister, and Hamas and Hezbollah representatives, while no high-level GCC officials and no Western countries were invited. IRGC chief Ahmad Vahidi — who surfaced from hiding July 2 — said 'You will take to your grave the dream of seeing this nation surrender,' Tehran warned the US and Israel against any attack during the funeral, and US national security adviser Mike Waltz publicly disparaged the late leader. A succession question sharpened as CNN reported the whereabouts of the newly named Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei (designated March 9) remain unknown — he has not appeared publicly since taking the post, raising open questions over his health and who is actually running Iran. US-Iran talks stayed paused for the funeral week, to resume 'at the earliest possible time' afterward. On the Strait, Iran's deputy foreign minister issued a 'serious warning' to France and the UK over military movements in Hormuz and Iran's ambassador to China reiterated Tehran will levy 'service fees' on transit once the 60-day toll-free window ends in mid-August, while the UK and France pledged to work with Oman to ensure 'safe transit for ships of all nations,' with reports of a possible Franco-British-led multinational freedom-of-navigation mission and Oman agreeing to cooperate. Oil markets were closed for the US Independence Day weekend (last print Brent ~$72/bbl on July 3, near pre-war levels, with Saudi and UAE crude exports recovered to about 90% of the pre-war baseline). The ground-invasion rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stays lifted (Day 17). No new strikes or shipping incidents were reported on July 4-5.
details: KHAMENEI FUNERAL ENTERS SECOND DAY; QOM PROCESSION JULY 5 (July 4-5, 2026): The coffin of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei lay in state at Tehran's Grand Mosalla on July 4 as mourners chanted 'revenge, revenge' and 'death to America' in ~100°F heat; authorities sprayed vaporized water on the crowds. July 5 was set for funeral prayers and a procession in Qom (Fatima Masoumeh shrine and Jamkaran mosque), with Najaf and Karbala (Iraq) on July 8 and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad on July 9. Officials project 15-20 million mourners over the six days — billed as the largest state funeral in Iranian history, exceeding Khomeini's 1989 rites (~10M). (CBS News; NPR; CNN; Wikipedia, July 4, 2026.)

FOREIGN DELEGATIONS AND HARD-LINE RHETORIC (July 4, 2026): Delegations from 70+ countries attended, including Russia (ex-president Dmitry Medvedev), Pakistan (PM Shehbaz Sharif), Iraq's president and prime minister, the Afghan Taliban foreign minister, and Hamas and Hezbollah representatives; no high-level GCC officials and no Western nations were invited. IRGC chief Ahmad Vahidi (who resurfaced from hiding July 2) said 'You will take to your grave the dream of seeing this nation surrender'; an army commander vowed to 'avenge the blood' of the slain leader; Iran warned the US and Israel against any attack during the funeral; and US NSA Mike Waltz publicly disparaged the late leader. (CBS News; Euronews; Al Jazeera, July 3-4, 2026.)

SUCCESSION QUESTION SHARPENS — NEW SUPREME LEADER'S WHEREABOUTS UNKNOWN (July 4, 2026): CNN reported that the whereabouts of Iran's new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei — named to succeed his father on March 9 — remain unknown; he has not appeared publicly since taking the post, fueling questions over his health, whether he would attend the funeral, and who is actually running Iran. (CNN, 'Whereabouts of Iran's new supreme leader unknown,' July 4, 2026.)

HORMUZ — IRAN WARNS FRANCE/UK, REAFFIRMS MID-AUGUST FEES; UK/FRANCE BACK OMAN (July 4, 2026): Iran's deputy foreign minister issued a 'serious warning' to France and the UK over military movements in the Strait, and Iran's ambassador to China reiterated Tehran will charge 'service fees' for Hormuz transit once the 60-day toll-free pause ends around mid-August. The UK and France pledged to work with Oman to ensure 'safe transit for ships of all nations,' with reports of a possible Franco-British-led multinational freedom-of-navigation mission and Oman agreeing to cooperate. US-Iran talks remained paused for the funeral week. (CBS News; GlobalSecurity/PressTV, July 3-4, 2026.)

OIL MARKETS CLOSED; LAST PRINT NEAR PRE-WAR LEVELS (July 3-5, 2026): US commodity and financial markets were closed for the Independence Day weekend, so no fresh oil settlement printed on July 4-5. The last trade (Fri July 3) held Brent near $72/bbl (intraday ~$71.30-72.49), close to late-February pre-war levels, as Saudi crude exports rebounded to ~90% of the pre-war baseline alongside a UAE recovery and gradual Hormuz reopening. Hormuz tanker traffic continued its uneven recovery (43 transits July 1; well below the ~84/day pre-crisis baseline), with many vessels running with AIS off. (HDFCSky; TradingEconomics; Wikipedia/PortWatch, July 1-3, 2026.)

HORMUZ-AFFECTED ECONOMIES (early July 2026): India's Russian-crude imports hit a record ~2.66M bpd in June and India began exporting gasoline to Russia amid Russia's own fuel shortage; European benchmark gas (TTF) hovered ~€43/MWh with EU storage ~48% full (below the five-year average) on US-Iran talk optimism; Japan and South Korea continued oil-supply cooperation and non-Gulf sourcing. No discrete July 4-5 escalation in these economies. (Al Jazeera; Reuters; Trading Economics, July 1-3, 2026.)

alternate_readings.reading: The unexplained public absence of the new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei during his father's massive state funeral reads two ways from the same facts. One reading treats it as deliberate security prudence and Shia mourning protocol — a wartime leadership keeping its principal out of a predictable, crowd-dense target set after the Feb 28 decapitation strike, with real authority exercised through the Supreme National Security Council and the IRGC as designed. The other reading treats the months-long non-appearance since his March 9 designation as evidence of a genuine leadership vacuum or incapacity — that Mojtaba may be gravely unwell, sidelined, or a figurehead, and that the IRGC and security establishment are effectively running Iran, which would bear on who can actually deliver on any US-Iran deal.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings rest on the same on-record facts: Mojtaba Khamenei was named successor March 9; he has not appeared publicly since; his whereabouts were unknown as the funeral opened (CNN, July 4); and it was unclear whether he would attend. Which reading is correct depends on non-public information about his health, location, and actual decision-making role — none of it determinable from open sources today.

daily_entries.headline: RUSSIA-UKRAINE — JULY 4-5: KOSTIANTYNIVKA CONTROL CONTESTED. RUSSIA'S GENERAL-STAFF CHIEF GERASIMOV TOLD PUTIN (JULY 3) THAT RUSSIAN FORCES HAD 'LIBERATED' KOSTIANTYNIVKA — A KEY SLOVIANSK-KRAMATORSK-KOSTIANTYNIVKA DEFENSIVE HUB — AND PUTIN HAILED IT; ON JULY 4 ZELENSKY AND UKRAINE'S GENERAL STAFF FLATLY DENIED IT ('ANOTHER RUSSIAN LIE'), WITH ZELENSKY CHALLENGING PUTIN TO MEET HIM IN THE CITY. ISW ASSESSED NO CONFIRMED ADVANCES JULY 3 AND CONTINUES TO CHARACTERIZE GAINS AS SMALL-GROUP INFILTRATION, NOT CONSOLIDATED CONTROL. UKRAINE STRUCK THE ST. PETERSBURG OIL TERMINAL AND MILITARY TARGETS AT KRONSTADT (JULY 4, ~1,100 KM — ONE OF THE DEEPEST STRIKES YET ON PUTIN'S HOME CITY), PART OF A CAMPAIGN THAT HAS HIT 8 OF RUSSIA'S TOP 10 REFINERIES IN 2026. RUSSIA CONTINUED MASS STRIKES (OVERNIGHT ATTACKS INJURED ~23 IN KYIV; A JULY 4 DRONE HIT A POLTAVA GAS FACILITY), AFTER THE JULY 1-2 KYIV BARRAGE (74 MISSILES + 496 DRONES, 20-31 KILLED). A ~40-MINUTE ZELENSKY-TRUMP CALL (JULY 4) — 'THE BEST CONVERSATION IN ALL THIS TIME' — AGREED TO STRENGTHEN UKRAINE'S AIR DEFENSES AND EXPAND JOINT DRONE/WEAPONS PRODUCTION, DAYS AFTER A US DEFENSE DEPARTMENT PAUSE ON PATRIOT AND PRECISION-ARTILLERY SHIPMENTS. NO US GROUND-DEPLOYMENT SURGE.
daily_entries.summary: The Russia-Ukraine war stayed at a grinding, no-breakthrough tempo over July 4-5, with a sharp information contest over Kostiantynivka. On July 3 Russia's General Staff chief Gen. Valery Gerasimov reported to Putin — filmed at a command post — that Russian forces had 'liberated' Kostiantynivka, calling it one of the main defensive hubs of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk-Kostiantynivka fortified area, and said forces were closing on Lyman; Putin hailed it as a strategic achievement and Russia's MoD posted flag-planting images. On July 4 President Zelensky and Ukraine's General Staff flatly denied the claim — 'It is just another Russian lie' — and Zelensky challenged Putin to meet him in Kostiantynivka if Russia truly held it. ISW assessed no confirmed advances on July 3 and continues to characterize Russian progress there as small-group infiltration (~50 m/day) rather than consolidated control; the Pokrovsk sector remained the heaviest, with Ukraine reporting 22 assaults repelled and 268 combat engagements along the front (July 3, per the General Staff), against Russian use of 1 missile, 93 airstrikes, 273 guided bombs and ~10,100 attack drones over the day. Ukraine extended its long-range energy-strike campaign, hitting the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and military targets at Kronstadt on July 4 (~1,100 km, among the deepest strikes yet on Putin's home city) — part of a 2026 campaign Zelensky calls a '40-day blitz' that RBC-Ukraine says has struck 8 of Russia's top 10 refineries. Russia continued mass strikes on Ukraine: after the July 1-2 Kyiv barrage (74 missiles and 496 drones; 20-31 killed, 90-100+ injured), overnight attacks into July 4 injured at least 23 more in Kyiv and a July 4 Russian drone hit a Naftogaz gas-production facility in Poltava region. Diplomacy stayed stalled — no new round July 4-5, with Putin still insisting on the 2022 Istanbul Protocols — but a roughly 40-minute Zelensky-Trump call on July 4 (which Zelensky called 'the best conversation in all this time, extremely productive') agreed to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and expand joint drone and weapons production, days after a US Defense Department pause on shipments of Patriot missiles and precision-guided artillery; Zelensky also spoke with Chancellor Merz, naming Patriot interceptors the top priority. Russia holds ~20% of Ukraine with no confirmed net change July 3-4; a widely cited think-tank estimate put total war casualties above 2 million, including as many as 600,000 deaths. The theatre continues to stress US bandwidth but triggered no US ground-deployment surge.
details: KOSTIANTYNIVKA — CAPTURE CLAIMED AND DENIED (July 3-4, 2026): Gen. Gerasimov told Putin on July 3 that Russian forces had 'liberated' Kostiantynivka and were closing on Lyman; Russia's MoD posted flag images. On July 4 Zelensky and Ukraine's General Staff denied it as 'another Russian lie,' and Zelensky challenged Putin to meet him in the city. ISW assessed no confirmed advances July 3 and continues to describe gains as small-group infiltration, not consolidated control. (Reuters via Moscow Times/US News; Mezha; ISW/Kyiv Post, July 3-4, 2026.)

FRONTLINE TEMPO (July 3-4, 2026): The Pokrovsk sector stayed heaviest — 22 Russian assaults repelled near Nykanorivka, Novooleksandrivka, Hryshyne, Rodynske, Kotlyne, Udachne and toward Myrnohrad. 268 combat engagements along the front (July 3, per the General Staff as of 08:00 July 4); Russia used 1 missile, 93 airstrikes, 273 guided bombs and ~10,106 attack drones. Clashes and a Russian airstrike also hit the Huliaipole/Zaporizhzhia direction. (Ukrinform; liveuamap, July 4, 2026.)

UKRAINE STRIKES ST. PETERSBURG OIL TERMINAL AND KRONSTADT (July 4, 2026): A major Ukrainian long-range drone strike hit the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal (Great Port; one of Russia's largest fuel-storage/export facilities) and military targets at Kronstadt (~1,100 km from Ukraine) — one of the deepest strikes yet on Putin's home city. Zelensky confirmed the strike; RBC-Ukraine reports Ukraine has hit 8 of Russia's top 10 refineries in 2026, driving a Russian fuel crisis. (Kyiv Independent; Al Jazeera, July 4, 2026.)

RUSSIAN MASS STRIKES CONTINUE (July 1-4, 2026): After the July 1-2 Kyiv barrage (74 missiles + 496 drones; 20-31 killed, 90-100+ injured, a nine-storey block partially collapsed), Putin vowed July 3 to 'continue' large-scale strikes; overnight attacks into July 4 injured at least 23 in Kyiv, and a July 4 Russian drone struck a Naftogaz gas-production facility in Poltava region, causing a fire. (Al Jazeera; Kyiv Independent; RFE/RL; Naftogaz, July 1-4, 2026.)

ZELENSKY-TRUMP CALL; US PATRIOT PAUSE (July 4, 2026): A ~40-minute Zelensky-Trump call — which Zelensky called 'the best conversation in all this time, extremely productive' — agreed to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses, hold a teams-level meeting, and cooperate on joint weapons production, drone tech and mutual investment. It followed a US Defense Department pause on shipments of Patriot missiles and precision-guided artillery to Ukraine; Zelensky also spoke with Chancellor Merz, naming Patriot interceptors the top priority. No US ground-deployment surge occurred. (Kyiv Independent; Newsweek; Kyiv Post, July 4, 2026.)

alternate_readings.reading: Whether Russia controls Kostiantynivka reads two opposite ways from the same July 3-4 record. Ukraine's reading (Zelensky, General Staff): the claim is 'another Russian lie' — Ukrainian forces are still contesting the city, gains are small-group infiltration without consolidated control, and Zelensky's public challenge to Putin to 'meet me there' is meant to expose the claim as propaganda.

Independent verification of who physically holds the city is not available from open sources in real time, and battlefield control there has been fluid.

daily_entries.summary: In Venezuela, acting President Delcy Rodríguez's 180-day interim mandate — she was sworn in January 5, 2026 after Nicolás Maduro's US capture — formally expired on July 4, with no immediate government statement on what follows. The National Assembly, controlled by her party, could extend the mandate for 90 days or declare the presidency vacant and trigger a snap election; opposition leader María Corina Machado is pressing to return. The expiry lands amid an acute post-earthquake crisis: twin June 24 quakes in La Guaira killed at least 2,295, the US mobilized roughly 2,000 personnel and pledged $100M in aid, and Rodríguez has faced mounting criticism over the response (she issued the government's first public defense of it on July 3). Separately, the SDNY narcoterrorism trial of Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores — both of whom pleaded not guilty in January — was again delayed, from June 30 to July 22, with no trial date set. No new July 4-5 development surfaced in Cuba (the ongoing US fuel blockade and grid crisis continue, last major reporting mid-May) or in Colombia beyond World Cup coverage. This theatre remains a Western-Hemisphere political/humanitarian story with no direct bearing on the Iran ground-invasion track.

daily_entries.headline: DAY 128 — CEASEFIRE DAY 88 / US BLOCKADE LIFTED DAY 16 — THE WAR MOVED FULLY OFF THE KINETIC TRACK AND INTO TWO PARALLEL PROCESSES: A PAUSED US-IRAN NEGOTIATION AND A SIX-DAY STATE FUNERAL FOR SLAIN SUPREME LEADER KHAMENEI. daily_entries.summary: The Iran war on July 1-4 ran entirely on the diplomatic and ceremonial register, not the ground one. The July 1-2 US-Iran round in Doha (indirect, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan; Witkoff and Kushner present on the US side) concluded with Qatar reporting 'positive progress' but no breakthrough toward lasting peace. Negotiators produced implementation mechanics from the June 17 MOU — a goods-purchase channel for the first tranche of frozen Iranian assets (reports of ~$3B for humanitarian goods; US officials denied any final understanding was reached), a communications channel to flag and address ceasefire violations, and an agreed focus on restoring reliable Hormuz passage — while the core disputes stayed open: the US rejects any Iranian-led toll regime and Tehran asserts joint Iran-Oman sovereignty over the corridor and plans tolls from mid-August; no frozen funds actually moved; and the nuclear-inspections dispute persists, with Speaker Ghalibaf denying IAEA access to the US-bombed Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan sites (offering only Bushehr and Tehran). Trump said 'denuclearisation of Iran is moving along well' and 'I think they've come a long way'; VP Vance said nuclear issues would be 'addressed later' and warned that if Iran tries to rebuild its nuclear program 'that's going to change our calculus.' The US agreed to halt talks for a week, postponing the next round until after the funeral. On July 4 Iran opened a six-day state funeral for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei — killed in the Feb 28 US-Israeli opening strike and buried only now after repeated wartime postponement — lying in state at Tehran's Grand Mosalla (July 4-5) ahead of a Tehran procession (July 6), Qom (July 7), Najaf and Karbala in Iraq (July 8) and burial in Mashhad (July 9); officials expect 15-20 million mourners, the largest state funeral in Iranian history, with delegations from about 30 countries including Russia (Dmitry Medvedev as Putin's 'special emissary') and China. Iran's joint military command warned all oil tankers must follow Tehran-designated Hormuz routes or face a 'forceful response,' and a foreign container ship reportedly ran aground outside the Iranian-designated corridor. Oil fell to a four-month low (Brent about $71.5/bbl on July 3, down ~0.4%), far below the wartime peaks above $110 and the $130+ a US ground commitment would imply. The ground-invasion rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stays lifted (Day 16) and the USS Boxer ARG stays disaggregated. The only US military event of the week was a non-combat mishap: a US Navy helicopter made an emergency water landing in the Arabian Sea, with one crew member reported missing.
details: DOHA ROUND CONCLUDES WITH 'POSITIVE PROGRESS,' NO BREAKTHROUGH (July 1-2, 2026): The US-Iran round in Doha — held indirectly through Qatari and Pakistani mediators, with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner present — concluded July 2. VP JD Vance said on July 1 the talks were 'going well.' Qatar's spokesman reported 'positive progress' on technical matters; negotiators focused on Hormuz maritime traffic and unfreezing Iranian funds — issues both sides had previously indicated were largely resolved — rather than the core disagreements, yielding no apparent breakthrough toward lasting peace. (CNN; Al Jazeera; The National, July 1-2, 2026.)

IMPLEMENTATION STEPS AGREED, CORE DISPUTES UNRESOLVED (July 2, 2026): The round produced a goods-purchase mechanism for the first tranche of frozen assets (reports of a ~$3B humanitarian-goods arrangement; US officials denied any understanding was finalized), a communications channel to flag and address ceasefire violations, and an agreed focus on restoring reliable Hormuz passage. But the sessions stayed indirect throughout; the toll dispute is unresolved (Washington rejects any Iranian-led fee mechanism, Tehran asserts joint sovereignty over the corridor with Oman); no frozen funds actually moved; and the nuclear-inspection dispute persists. (Al Jazeera; The National, July 2, 2026.)

NUCLEAR-INSPECTIONS STANDOFF PERSISTS (July 2, 2026): Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf denied IAEA access to the US-bombed nuclear sites (Fordow, Natanz, Isfahan), saying inspectors would reach only Bushehr and Tehran facilities. Trump said 'denuclearisation of Iran is moving along well' and later 'I think they've come a long way'; sources said nuclear matters were absent from the technical discussions, with VP Vance saying the issue would be 'addressed later' and warning that if Iran tries to rebuild its nuclear program 'that's going to change our calculus.' (Al Jazeera; The Bridge Chronicle, July 2, 2026.)

US HALTS TALKS FOR A WEEK; NEXT ROUND AFTER FUNERAL (July 3, 2026): Mediators Qatar and Pakistan said the next negotiation round would resume 'at the earliest possible time' after Khamenei's funeral ceremonies conclude; the US agreed to pause talks for roughly a week. No specific date for the resumption was set. (Fox News Digital; CBS News, July 3, 2026.)

IRAN OPENS SIX-DAY STATE FUNERAL FOR KHAMENEI (July 3-4, 2026): Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's coffin was placed on display at Tehran's Grand Mosalla on July 3 ahead of a six-day funeral beginning July 4 — lying in state in Tehran July 4-5, a Tehran procession July 6, ceremonies in Qom July 7, processions in Najaf and Karbala (Iraq) July 8, and burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad on July 9. Officials expect 15-20 million mourners, which would make it the largest state funeral in Iranian history; First VP Mohammad Reza Aref called it 'the most important event of this century.' The funeral had been postponed repeatedly since early March because of the war. (Al Jazeera; TIME; CNN, July 3, 2026.)

FOREIGN DELEGATIONS AND HARD-LINE RHETORIC (July 3-4, 2026): Delegations from about 30 countries were expected, including Russia — former president Dmitry Medvedev attending as Vladimir Putin's 'special emissary' — and China, plus Palestinian and Lebanese militant-group representatives. Iranian General Ahmad Vahidi said 'You will take to your grave the dream of seeing this nation surrender'; Tehran warned of 'harsh retaliation' against the US as the funeral opened, while US national security adviser Mike Waltz publicly disparaged the late leader. (CBS News; Fox News Digital, July 3, 2026.)

IRAN ENFORCES HORMUZ ROUTES; TRAFFIC RECOVERS (July 2-3, 2026): Iran's joint military command warned that all oil tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz must use its approved routes or face a 'forceful response,' and Iranian state media reported a foreign container ship ran aground in shallow water outside the Iran-designated corridor. Traffic kept recovering — 258 vessels transited in the prior week, up from 138 the week before, still far below the pre-war ~130/day — as major container lines resumed Gulf services. Iran reiterated it will impose transit tolls from mid-August once the MOU's toll-free window expires. (CBS News; Gulf News; The Bridge Chronicle, July 2-3, 2026.)

OIL AT FOUR-MONTH LOW; NON-COMBAT US NAVY MISHAP (July 2-3, 2026): Brent crude extended its decline, sliding to about $71.54/bbl on July 3 (-0.36%) — a four-month low — as easing Middle East tensions and the gradual Hormuz reopening reduced supply-disruption fears; Trump's remarks that Iran had 'come a long way' contributed to the drop. Separately, a US Navy helicopter made an emergency water landing in the Arabian Sea, with one crew member reported missing — a non-combat mishap, not a ground-operation indicator. Over 640,000 displaced Lebanese have returned home amid the ceasefire. (TradingEconomics/CNBC; Gulf News; CBS News, July 2-3, 2026.)

The deal-durability open question (iran-us-deal-reached-june-2026) stays live — the round produced 'positive progress' but no breakthrough, the talks are only paused for the funeral week, and the toll and nuclear-inspection disputes are unresolved — and the Hormuz-governance question (iran-hormuz-administration-tolls-dispute-june-2026) is unresolved, with Iran now setting a mid-August toll deadline the US rejects. alternate_readings.reading: The July 1-2 Doha round reads two ways from the same facts. One reading treats the 'positive progress,' the goods-purchase mechanism, the violations-deconfliction channel and the Hormuz-passage focus as real forward motion on the MOU — the ceasefire holding, both sides institutionalizing de-escalation and deferring the hard questions to a next round. The other reading treats it as a stall dressed as progress: the sessions were indirect throughout, negotiators revisited issues 'both sides had previously indicated were largely resolved' rather than the core disputes, no frozen funds actually moved, the toll and nuclear-inspection disputes are openly unresolved, Iran set a mid-August toll deadline the US flatly rejects, and the round ended with talks merely paused for a funeral week rather than scheduled to reconvene.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings rest on the same on-record facts: Qatar's 'positive progress' statement; the reported goods-purchase mechanism, comms channel and Hormuz-passage focus; the US denial that any frozen-asset understanding was finalized; Ghalibaf's denial of IAEA access to the bombed sites; Iran's mid-August toll assertion and the US rejection of any Iranian-led toll regime; and the agreement to halt talks for a week with no fixed resumption date. Which reading prevails depends on whether the next round convenes after the funeral, whether the goods-purchase/asset tranche actually moves, and whether the toll and inspection disputes are bridged — none resolvable from open sources today.

daily_entries.summary: The US-Iran round in Doha concluded July 2 after two days of indirect talks mediated by Qatar and Pakistan. Qatar reported 'positive progress' on technical matters but the sides reached no breakthrough toward lasting peace, focusing on Hormuz maritime traffic and unfreezing Iranian funds — issues both had previously indicated were largely resolved. The round yielded implementation mechanics: a goods-purchase mechanism for the first tranche of frozen assets (reports of a ~$3B humanitarian-goods arrangement, though US officials denied any understanding was finalized), a communications channel to flag and address violations, and an agreed focus on restoring Hormuz passage. But the core disputes stayed open: Washington rejects any Iranian-led toll regime while Tehran asserts joint sovereignty over the corridor with Oman and plans to impose tolls from mid-August; no frozen funds actually moved; and the nuclear-inspections dispute persists, with Speaker Ghalibaf denying IAEA access to the US-bombed Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan sites (offering only Bushehr and Tehran). Trump said 'denuclearisation of Iran is moving along well' and 'I think they've come a long way,' contributing to oil's slide; VP Vance said nuclear issues would be 'addressed later.' Iran's military warned tankers to use its designated Hormuz routes, and a foreign container ship reportedly ran aground outside the corridor. Oil extended its decline toward a four-month low. The ground rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side: no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the blockade stays lifted (Day 14) and the USS Boxer ARG stays disaggregated.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 30 (Day 124): The three-day breach-retaliation cycle that had broadened on June 28 to direct Iran-on-US-base strikes reversed back into de-escalation on June 29. A US official said the US and Iran had agreed to 'stand down' after trading strikes over the weekend and to let vessels 'move freely' through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that 'no drones or missiles launched by Iran at US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait last night reached their targets.' President Trump posted on Truth Social that 'Iran has requested a meeting' and that 'it will take place tomorrow in Doha' (Tuesday, June 30); the talks — originally planned for Switzerland — were relocated to Qatar and re-scoped to the Hormuz standoff. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would travel to Doha for 'high-level meetings' held alongside 'technical talks.' Iran's deputy foreign minister and senior negotiator Kazem Gharibabadi told IRNA that no technical working-group meetings had been scheduled 'for this week,' leaving initial uncertainty over Iranian participation. Separately, Iran and Oman held their first meeting on managing the reopened Strait, though disagreements persisted over corridor management and demining: Iran's deputy FM said Iran would conduct demining alone and rejected international involvement (including a France-Oman joint demining initiative), calling the situation 'sensitive and complex,' while Oman rejected proposed Iranian transit fees and the GCC secretary-general called tolls 'not acceptable.' Iran's president announced Tehran had received $6 billion of the total $12 billion of Iranian resources held in Qatar under the MOU, with reports that the unfrozen funds were earmarked to buy American wheat and corn. Markets read it as de-escalation: Brent rose only marginally to about $69.70/bbl on June 29, rebounding slightly off a four-month low (Brent had hit ~$72 on June 26, its lowest since Feb 27); Trump said oil prices were 'charging down' after the Hormuz reopening. Hormuz traffic remained thinned by the weekend clashes (29 vessels Saturday, 12 Sunday, down from 70 the prior Wednesday) but major container lines resumed Gulf services and the first commercial flight from Tehran landed in Dubai. On the Lebanon track, the Lebanese army chief held talks with a US military commander on security. The ground rung was unchanged: the day's US-side move was diplomatic (a stand-down plus the Doha meeting), not a ground operation — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 12) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. (NPR; CNBC; NBC News; CBS News; Euronews; Times of Israel; The National; TradingEconomics, June 29, 2026.)

Hormuz traffic stayed thinned by the weekend clashes — 29 commodity vessels crossed Saturday and 12 Sunday, down from 70 the prior Wednesday — but major container lines resumed Gulf services and the first commercial flight from Tehran landed in Dubai. David Hazutt) was killed in southern Lebanon and after Hezbollah rejected the June 26 Israel-Lebanon framework as 'null and void.' No US ground forces were involved. (The National, June 29, 2026.)

daily_entries.prediction_impact: The June 29 stand-down and the announced June 30 Doha talks reverse the three-day breach-retaliation cycle back toward de-escalation, leaving Predictive History's imminent-US-ground-invasion and Hormuz-and-Kharg-seizure thesis disconfirmed-and-inverted. After the cycle's June 28 peak (a US 10-target airstrike near Hormuz and Iran's missile/drone strike on US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain), both sides agreed to halt attacks and route the dispute back into diplomacy — a stand-down, a fresh high-level meeting in Doha, an Iran-Oman Hormuz-management track, a partial ($6B of $12B) frozen-asset release, and oil falling toward a four-month low. The US instrument remained diplomatic and air/naval, never a landing, a Kharg assault, an ARG/MEU surge, or a draft; the blockade stayed lifted (Day 12) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. The structural inversion holds: the chokepoint is being reopened and governed by negotiation (Iran-Oman talks; toll dispute) rather than US seizure. The episode keeps the deal-durability open question (iran-us-deal-reached-june-2026) live — the Gharibabadi-vs-Trump contradiction over whether the Doha meeting convenes is the immediate test — and the Hormuz-governance question (iran-hormuz-administration-tolls-dispute-june-2026) unresolved (Iran demining alone / tolls vs Oman-GCC rejection). But any renewed collapse would return the war to the air/missile/maritime register, not vindicate a ground invasion.

alternate_readings.reading: The June 29 developments read two ways from the same facts. One reading treats the mutual stand-down, the announced Doha meeting, the Iran-Oman Hormuz talks and the $6B asset release as a genuine return to the de-escalation track — the breach-retaliation cycle spent, both sides choosing diplomacy over a fourth day of strikes. The other reading treats it as a fragile, possibly cosmetic pause: Iran's own deputy FM publicly denied any talks were scheduled even as Trump announced them, the core Hormuz-governance and demining disputes remain unresolved, traffic is still far below normal, and only half the frozen funds were released — so the 'deal' is being held together by contradictory public statements that could unravel at the next incident.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings rest on the same on-record facts (the US-official stand-down statement; Trump's Truth Social announcement of a Tuesday Doha meeting with Witkoff and Kushner; Gharibabadi's IRNA denial that technical talks were scheduled; the Iran-Oman first meeting with unresolved corridor/demining disputes; Iran's rejection of France-Oman demining; the Oman/GCC rejection of tolls; the $6B-of-$12B release). Which reading prevails depends on whether the Doha meeting actually convenes on June 30, whether it produces movement on Hormuz governance, and whether the stand-down holds — none resolvable from open sources today.
public_assertion_by: US (Trump; press secretary Karoline Leavitt; US official): the two sides agreed to 'stand down,' vessels will move freely, 'Iran has requested a meeting,' and it 'will take place tomorrow in Doha' with Witkoff and Kushner attending 'high-level meetings.'

Iran (deputy FM/negotiator Kazem Gharibabadi): 'the holding of technical meetings of the working groups has not been scheduled for this week'; Iran will demine the Strait alone and rejects international involvement; the situation is 'sensitive and complex.'
Oman / GCC: rejected Iran's proposed transit tolls as 'not acceptable' and affirmed commitment to international maritime law.
alternate_readings.why_unresolvable: It is not yet known whether the June 30 Doha meeting will actually convene given Iran's public denial, whether it will move the Hormuz-governance and demining disputes, or whether the stand-down will hold — all forward-looking and undeterminable from open sources today.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 29 (Day 123): The breach-retaliation cycle that opened June 25-26 and repeated June 27 entered a third straight day on June 28 and broadened qualitatively — from US-on-Iran and Iran-on-shipping strikes to a direct Iranian missile-and-drone attack on US bases in the Gulf, the first such Iran-on-US-base strikes since June 10-11. After the June 27 Iranian drone attack on the tanker M/T Kiku, US Central Command said it 'conducted strikes on 10 Iranian military targets at multiple locations in and near the Strait of Hormuz' (reported sites: Sirik, Bandar-e Lengeh and Qeshm Island), hitting 'military surveillance infrastructure, communication systems, air defense sites, drone storage facilities, and minelayer capabilities.' Iran's IRGC then said it fired ballistic missiles and drones at the US Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait and the US Fifth Fleet headquarters (Port Salman) in Bahrain, claiming it 'destroyed eight important US military facilities'; a US official countered that all Iranian weapons 'were shot down, intercepted, or failed to reach their intended targets,' with 'no US injuries or impacts to American locations.' Qatar's Interior Ministry said one Qatari citizen was killed by shrapnel from the military operations and an Arab resident was injured but stable. Iran's IRGC warned that any further breach 'will lead to a complete halt of ongoing processes,' Iran's Foreign Ministry called the US strikes 'brutal attacks' violating the MOU, and Iran boycotted the scheduled technical talks; nonetheless a senior US administration official said 'technical talks with Iran on how to implement the memorandum of understanding are still planned for the coming days,' that 'no talks have been canceled,' and that 'both sides are still exchanging messages through deconfliction channels.' Trump said 'there may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable,' while FM Abbas Araghchi declared 'the Strait of Hormuz remains under the total oversight and management of Iran' and parliamentary security-commission chair Ebrahim Azizi cast Iran's strikes as 'ceasefire management' rather than a breach. Bahrain said the Iranian attacks 'undermined opportunities for de-escalation' and Kuwait condemned 'repeated heinous Iranian aggressions.' On the Lebanon track, an Israeli soldier (Capt. David Hazutt) was killed in southern Lebanon operations. Markets had repriced only modestly: Brent had ended the prior week near a four-month low (~$72/bbl, lowest since Feb 27); no confirmed June 28-29 settle was available in reporting as the weekend exchange unfolded. The ground rung was unchanged: every US response remained air/naval and every Iranian response air/missile/maritime — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 11) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. (Al Jazeera; RFE/RL; NPR; ABC News; CBS News; CNBC; Fox News Digital; Britannica '2026 Iran war,' June 27-28, 2026.)
details: CENTCOM STRIKES 10 IRANIAN TARGETS NEAR HORMUZ (June 28, 2026): US Central Command said it 'conducted strikes on 10 Iranian military targets at multiple locations in and near the Strait of Hormuz' in response to the June 27 Iranian drone attack on the M/T Kiku tanker. Reported sites included Sirik, Bandar-e Lengeh and Qeshm Island; CENTCOM said the strikes hit 'military surveillance infrastructure, communication systems, air defense sites, drone storage facilities, and minelayer capabilities.' This was again an air/naval-register strike package from existing in-theatre assets, not a ground operation. (Al Jazeera; NPR; CBS News, June 28, 2026.)

IRAN RETALIATES AGAINST US GULF BASES — FIRST SINCE JUNE 10-11 (June 28, 2026): Iran's IRGC said it launched ballistic missiles and drones at the US Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait and the US Fifth Fleet headquarters (Port Salman) in Bahrain, claiming it 'destroyed eight important US military facilities at the Ali al-Salem base in Kuwait and at the Fifth Fleet naval base.' A US official said all Iranian missiles and drones 'were shot down, intercepted, or failed to reach their intended targets,' with 'no US injuries or impacts to American locations.' This was the first Iranian strike on US Gulf bases since the June 10-11 barrage. (Al Jazeera; ABC News; CBS News, June 28, 2026.)

ONE QATARI CITIZEN KILLED (June 28, 2026): Qatar's Ministry of Interior said one Qatari citizen died from 'shrapnel wounds resulting from the military operations,' with an Arab resident injured and in stable condition — the first reported civilian fatality of the renewed breach-retaliation cycle. (Al Jazeera, June 28, 2026.)

IRAN THREATENS 'COMPLETE HALT,' BOYCOTTS TALKS; US SAYS TALKS 'STILL PLANNED' (June 28, 2026): Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that 'violating the ceasefire ... will lead to a complete halt of ongoing processes'; Iran's Foreign Ministry called the US strikes 'brutal attacks' violating the agreement and Iran boycotted the scheduled technical talks, questioning whether Washington had met its commitments on unfreezing funds. A senior US administration official countered that 'technical talks with Iran on how to implement the memorandum of understanding are still planned for the coming days,' that 'no talks have been canceled,' and that 'both sides are still exchanging messages through deconfliction channels.' (Al Jazeera; ABC News, June 28, 2026.)

RHETORIC HARDENS — TRUMP, ARAGHCHI, AZIZI (June 28, 2026): Trump said 'there may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable.' Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi declared 'the Strait of Hormuz remains under the total oversight and management of Iran.' Ebrahim Azizi, chair of Iran's parliamentary national security commission, characterized Iran's strikes as 'ceasefire management' rather than a breach. (Al Jazeera; RFE/RL, June 28, 2026.)

GULF STATES CONDEMN IRAN (June 28, 2026): Bahrain said the Iranian attacks 'undermined opportunities for de-escalation'; Kuwait condemned 'repeated heinous Iranian aggressions.' The condemnations extend the prior day's joint GCC/Bahrain/UAE/Kuwait censure of Iran's drone attacks on shipping. (Al Jazeera; RFE/RL, June 28, 2026.)

LEBANON — ISRAELI SOLDIER KILLED (June 28, 2026): On the war's chief secondary fault line, an Israeli soldier (Capt. David Hazutt) was killed in Israeli operations against Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon, a day after Hezbollah rejected the June 26 Israel-Lebanon framework as 'null and void.' No US ground forces were involved. (ABC News, June 28, 2026.)

OIL — RISK PREMIUM RE-ENTERS, NO CONFIRMED SETTLE (June 27-28, 2026): Brent had ended the prior week near a four-month low (~$72/bbl on June 26, its lowest since February 27, after an over-10% weekly drop) on supply-side de-escalation — Gulf exports back to ~75% of pre-war, Saudi loading resumed at Ras Tanura, Hormuz reopening. The broadened June 28 exchange (direct strikes on US Gulf bases) reintroduced risk premium, but no confirmed June 28-29 settle was available in reporting as the weekend unfolded; prices remained far below the $130+ a US ground commitment would imply. (CNBC; TradingEconomics; Al Jazeera Economy, June 26-28, 2026.)

GROUND RUNG UNCHANGED (June 29, 2026): Through a third day of the cycle — and its broadening to direct Iran-on-US-base strikes — every US response stayed air/naval and every Iranian response air/missile/maritime. No US troops in Iran, no Kharg Island assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 11) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. The escalation lever on both sides remained air/missile and maritime — not mobilization.
daily_entries.prediction_impact: The June 28 broadening of the breach-retaliation cycle is the most serious deal-durability stress since the MOU — a third straight day, a qualitative jump from shipping strikes to direct Iranian missile/drone attacks on US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, the first Gulf-state civilian fatality (a Qatari killed by shrapnel), an IRGC 'complete halt' threat, and an Iranian boycott of the technical talks. Yet it again ran entirely on the air/missile/maritime rung, leaving Predictive History's imminent-US-ground-invasion and Hormuz-and-Kharg-seizure thesis disconfirmed-and-inverted. The US instrument was again airstrikes (10 targets near Hormuz), not a landing, a Kharg assault, an ARG/MEU surge, or a draft; Iran's instrument was missiles/drones from its own territory, not a ground move; the blockade stayed lifted (Day 11) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. The structural inversion holds: Iran (not the US) keeps using force to assert coercive control — now striking US bases and reasserting 'total oversight and management' of the Strait — while the US keeps the chokepoint open. The episode sharply raises the 'fragile ceasefire could re-collapse' reading of the deal-durability open question (iran-us-deal-reached-june-2026) and the 'genuine, hardening sovereignty claim' reading of the Hormuz-governance question (iran-hormuz-administration-tolls-dispute-june-2026), and revives the Gulf-base-strike pattern tracked under (june3-kuwait-kinetic-escalation-2026). But a collapse, if it came, would return the war to the air/missile/maritime register — not vindicate a ground invasion.

alternate_readings.reading: The June 28 exchange is read two ways from the same facts. One reading treats Iran's strikes on US bases as a contained, face-saving 'ceasefire management' gesture inside a process both sides still want to preserve — telegraphed, fully intercepted, with no US casualties, framed by Tehran's own security-commission chair as management rather than breach, and immediately followed by a US insistence that talks are 'still planned' and deconfliction channels remain open. The other reading treats it as a decisive escalation that is breaking the ceasefire: the cycle now into a third day, broadened from ships to US bases, a Gulf civilian killed, an IRGC 'complete halt' threat, an Iranian boycott of the talks, and Trump warning the US may no longer 'be reasonable.'
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings draw on the same on-record facts (the June 28 CENTCOM 10-target strike; Iran's missile/drone attack on Ali Al Salem and the Fifth Fleet HQ; the US 'all intercepted / no injuries' account vs. the IRGC 'eight facilities destroyed' claim; the Qatari fatality; the 'complete halt' warning and talks boycott vs. the US 'talks still planned' statement; the Azizi 'ceasefire management' framing). Which prevails depends on whether the cycle continues, whether the boycotted talks actually reconvene, and whether either side acts on its escalation threats — none resolvable from open sources today.
public_assertion_by: US (CENTCOM; Trump; senior administration official): the 10-target strike was a justified response to Iran's attacks on shipping; all Iranian retaliation was intercepted with no US injuries; talks are 'still planned' and 'no talks have been canceled' — but 'there may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable.'

Iran (IRGC; FM Araghchi; security-commission chair Ebrahim Azizi): the US strikes are 'brutal attacks' violating the MOU; Iran 'destroyed eight important US military facilities'; the Strait is under Iran's 'total oversight and management'; the strikes were 'ceasefire management,' not a breach; further violations 'will lead to a complete halt of ongoing processes.'
Gulf states (Bahrain; Kuwait; Qatar): Iran's attacks 'undermined opportunities for de-escalation' and were 'repeated heinous Iranian aggressions'; Qatar reported one citizen killed.
alternate_readings.why_unresolvable: It is not yet known whether the breach-retaliation cycle will continue into a fourth day, whether Iran's 'complete halt' threat and talks boycott end the 60-day roadmap or prove a bargaining posture, or whether the US acts on Trump's 'no longer able to be reasonable' warning — all forward-looking and undeterminable from open sources today.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 29 (Day 123): The ground-invasion EXECUTION track produced no new indicator even as the conflict's breach-retaliation cycle entered a third straight day and broadened qualitatively on June 28. US Central Command said it struck 10 Iranian military targets in and near the Strait of Hormuz (reported sites Sirik, Bandar-e Lengeh, Qeshm Island) in response to the June 27 M/T Kiku drone attack; Iran's IRGC retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones against US bases in the Gulf — Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait and the US Fifth Fleet HQ (Port Salman) in Bahrain — the first Iranian strikes on US bases since June 10-11. A US official said all Iranian weapons were 'shot down, intercepted, or failed to reach their intended targets' with 'no US injuries,' though one Qatari civilian was killed by shrapnel. Critically for this tracker, the entire exchange ran on the air/missile/maritime rung: the US instrument was airstrikes from existing in-theatre assets, Iran's was missiles/drones from its own territory, and neither was a ground move. It remains the structural inverse of the predicted US seizure of the Strait — Iran (not the US) is using force to assert coercive control over Hormuz ('total oversight and management,' per Araghchi) while the US keeps the chokepoint open. Every US ground-execution indicator stayed at zero: no US troops in Iran, no Kharg Island assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 11) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. The live risk is deal durability — now sharply elevated by the cycle's third-day persistence, its broadening to US bases, a Gulf-state civilian fatality, an IRGC 'complete halt' threat and an Iranian talks boycott — but in the air/missile/maritime register, not a forming ground invasion. (Al Jazeera; RFE/RL; NPR; ABC News; CBS News, June 28, 2026.)
details: US RESPONSE WAS AGAIN AIR, NOT GROUND (June 28, 2026): CENTCOM's response to the M/T Kiku attack was a 10-target air/naval strike package near the Strait of Hormuz (surveillance, communications, air-defense, drone storage and minelayer capabilities), not a landing or a Kharg assault. No US ground forces entered Iran. (Al Jazeera; NPR; CBS News, June 28, 2026.)

The escalation was vertical (more targets, US bases) but stayed off the ground rung. (Al Jazeera; ABC News, June 28, 2026.)

STRUCTURAL INVERSION HARDENS (June 28, 2026): Iran reasserted that the Strait is under its 'total oversight and management' (Araghchi) and struck US Gulf bases, while the US kept Hormuz open, the blockade lifted (Day 11), and Gulf exports near ~75% of pre-war. daily_entries.prediction_impact: Day 123 keeps the ground-invasion execution thesis disconfirmed-and-inverted while marking the cycle's most serious escalation yet. The breakthrough event — Iran striking US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain — is exactly the kind of vertical escalation that could, in principle, precede a ground phase; instead it confirms the opposite dynamic, with both sides escalating within the air/missile/maritime register and neither moving ground forces. The blockade stays lifted, the Boxer ARG stays disaggregated, and there is no draft, no Kharg assault, and no new amphibious surge. Deal-durability risk is now high, but a collapse would resume the air/missile war, not initiate the predicted invasion.
