daily_entries.headline: DAY 122 — CEASEFIRE DAY 82 / US BLOCKADE LIFTED DAY 10 — THE BREACH-RETALIATION CYCLE REPEATED FOR A SECOND STRAIGHT DAY WITHOUT CROSSING ONTO THE GROUND RUNG. EARLY ON JUNE 27 AN IRANIAN ONE-WAY ATTACK DRONE HIT THE PANAMA-FLAGGED TANKER M/T KIKU (~2 MILLION BARRELS OF QATARI CRUDE BOUND FOR FUJAIRAH, UAE; BRIDGE DAMAGED, CREW SAFE, NO SPILL) AS IT TRANSITED NEAR THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ — AND FOR THE SECOND CONSECUTIVE NIGHT THE US LAUNCHED A FRESH, LARGER ROUND OF AIRSTRIKES ON IRAN ('A LARGER STRIKE THAN LAST NIGHT,' PER A SENIOR US OFFICIAL): CENTCOM SAID IT HIT IRANIAN AIR-DEFENSE AND SAM SYSTEMS, DRONE STORAGE, CRUISE MISSILES, TARGETING RADARS AND MINELAYER CAPABILITIES, ADDING 'U.S. FORCES REMAIN VIGILANT, LETHAL, AND READY.' VANCE REPEATED 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE.' IRAN CAST THE US STRIKES AS THE VIOLATION — MOHSEN REZAEI WARNED ANY BREACH WOULD DRAW A 'SWIFT AND DECISIVE' RESPONSE AND THE IRGC NAVY WARNED FUTURE US ATTACKS WOULD DRAW 'A BROADER RESPONSE THAN THIS.' BAHRAIN AND THE GCC CONDEMNED IRAN'S DRONE ATTACKS (BAHRAIN CALLED A DRONE STRIKE A VIOLATION OF ITS SOVEREIGNTY). HEZBOLLAH REJECTED THE JUNE 26 ISRAEL-LEBANON FRAMEWORK AS 'NULL AND VOID.' OIL STAYED IN DE-ESCALATION PRICING — BRENT BELOW $73/BBL (LOWEST SINCE FEB 27; >10% WEEKLY DROP, THE LARGEST IN A MONTH) AS GULF EXPORTS RECOVERED TO ~75% OF PRE-WAR. THE GROUND RUNG WAS UNCHANGED: BOTH US RESPONSES WERE AIR, NOT GROUND — NO US TROOPS IN IRAN, NO KHARG ASSAULT, NO NEW ARG/MEU, NO DRAFT; BLOCKADE STILL LIFTED (DAY 10), USS BOXER ARG DISAGGREGATED.
daily_entries.summary: JUNE 28 (Day 122): The breach-retaliation cycle that opened June 25-26 repeated for a second straight day, deepening the strain on the 60-day MOU without crossing onto the ground rung. Early on June 27 an Iranian one-way attack drone struck the Panama-flagged tanker M/T Kiku at about 4:30 a.m. ET as it transited near the Strait of Hormuz carrying more than two million barrels of Qatari crude bound for the UAE port of Fujairah; the vessel's bridge was damaged, all crew were reported safe, and no environmental damage occurred. In response — for the second consecutive night — US Central Command launched a fresh and larger round of airstrikes on Iran; a senior US official said 'it's a larger strike than last night,' and CENTCOM said the strikes hit Iranian air-defense and surface-to-air missile systems, drone storage facilities, cruise missiles, targeting radars and minelayer capabilities, adding that 'U.S. forces remain vigilant, lethal, and ready.' VP JD Vance reiterated 'Iran signed a ceasefire agreement. We have honored it... violence will be met with violence.' Iran framed the US strikes as the violation: senior official Mohsen Rezaei said 'the response to the violation of any article... will be swift and decisive,' the IRGC said the US had 'attacked the coasts of the Islamic Republic of Iran' over a vessel using 'an unauthorized route,' and the IRGC Navy warned that any future US attack would draw 'a broader response than this.' Bahrain condemned an early-Saturday Iranian drone strike as a violation of its sovereignty, and Bahrain, the UAE, Kuwait and the Gulf Cooperation Council jointly condemned Iran's drone attacks on shipping. On the Lebanon track, Hezbollah rejected the June 26 Israel-Lebanon framework as 'null and void,' and an Israeli strike on Nabatieh killed one a day after the framework was announced. Markets stayed in de-escalation pricing despite the two-day exchange: Brent had fallen below $73/bbl on June 26 — its lowest since February 27 and an over-10% weekly drop, the largest in a month — as Gulf exports recovered to roughly 75% of pre-war levels (~4.8 million bpd through Hormuz, the highest since the war began on Feb 28) and Saudi Arabia resumed loading crude at its Ras Tanura terminal; the US-Navy Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) announced a widened Hormuz transit route near Oman on June 27. Trump confirmed the Strait remains open and traffic continues. The ground rung was unchanged: for the second day running the US answered an Iranian maritime strike with air power, not ground forces — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 10) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. (CNBC; Fox News Digital; Al Jazeera; NBC News; ABC News; CBS News, June 27, 2026.)
details: SECOND US AIRSTRIKE IN AS MANY DAYS — 'LARGER THAN LAST NIGHT' (June 27, 2026): For the second consecutive night, US Central Command launched airstrikes on Iran in retaliation for an Iranian attack on shipping. A senior US official told reporters 'it's a larger strike than last night.' CENTCOM said the strikes hit Iranian military surveillance infrastructure, communication systems, air-defense and surface-to-air missile systems, drone storage facilities, cruise missiles, targeting radars and minelayer capabilities, and that the strikes were 'directed by President Trump'; 'U.S. forces remain vigilant, lethal, and ready.' These were again air/naval-register strikes from existing in-theatre assets, not a ground operation. (CNBC; Fox News Digital; ABC News; Al Jazeera, June 27, 2026.)

THE JUNE 27 ATTACK — M/T KIKU (June 27, 2026): An Iranian one-way attack drone hit the Panama-flagged tanker M/T Kiku at about 4:30 a.m. ET as it transited near the Strait of Hormuz carrying more than two million barrels of Qatari crude bound for the UAE port of Fujairah; the vessel reported being struck by a projectile, its bridge was damaged, all crew were reported safe, and there was no environmental damage. It was the second Iranian strike on shipping in three days, after the June 25 drone hit on the M/V Ever Lovely. (CNBC; Fox News Digital, June 27, 2026.)

IRAN: 'SWIFT AND DECISIVE' / 'A BROADER RESPONSE' (June 27, 2026): Iran cast the US strikes as the violation. Senior official Mohsen Rezaei said 'the response to the violation of any article [of the memorandum]... will be swift and decisive.' The IRGC said the US 'violated its commitments and, under various pretexts, attacked the coasts of the Islamic Republic of Iran with an airstrike due to the passage of a violating ship through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz,' and the IRGC Navy warned that any future US attack would draw 'a broader response than this.' (CBS News; Fox News Digital; Al Jazeera, June 27, 2026.)

GULF STATES CONDEMN IRAN; BAHRAIN CITES SOVEREIGNTY (June 27, 2026): Bahrain condemned an early-Saturday Iranian drone strike as a violation of its sovereignty. Bahrain, the UAE, Kuwait and the Gulf Cooperation Council jointly condemned Iran's drone attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. (Fox News Digital, June 27, 2026.)

LEBANON — HEZBOLLAH REJECTS FRAMEWORK AS 'NULL AND VOID' (June 27, 2026): A day after Rubio announced the June 26 Israel-Lebanon framework (Hezbollah excluded), Hezbollah rejected the agreement as 'null and void.' An Israeli strike on Lebanon's Nabatieh killed one person, one day after the framework was announced — the fragile Lebanon track persisting as the war's chief secondary fault line. (Fox News Digital; Al Jazeera, June 27, 2026.)

OIL STAYS IN DE-ESCALATION PRICING DESPITE THE EXCHANGE (June 26-27, 2026): Brent fell below $73/bbl on June 26 — its lowest since February 27 — and posted an over-10% weekly drop, the largest in a month, even through the two-day kinetic exchange. Each strike produced only a brief, partial rebound. The structural drivers were supply-side de-escalation: Gulf exports recovered to roughly 75% of pre-war levels, Saudi Arabia resumed loading tankers at its Ras Tanura terminal, and the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar boosted output. The price action is the inverse of the sustained $130+ a US ground commitment would imply. (CNBC; TradingEconomics; Al Jazeera Economy, June 26-27, 2026.)

HORMUZ KEEPS REOPENING — JMIC WIDENED ROUTE (June 27, 2026): Oil flows through the Strait rose to roughly 4.8 million bpd since the US-Iran deal — the highest since the war began on Feb 28, though still well below the ~15 million bpd of pre-war transits. The US-Navy Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) announced a widened route through the Strait near Oman, allowing increased naval traffic in both directions; Trump confirmed the Strait remains open and traffic continues. (CNBC; 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis timeline; RFE/RL, June 24-27, 2026.)

GROUND RUNG UNCHANGED (June 28, 2026): For the second day running, the US answered an Iranian maritime strike with air power, not ground forces. Every US ground-execution indicator stayed at zero: no US troops in Iran, no Kharg Island assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no draft; the naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 10) and the USS Boxer ARG stayed disaggregated. The escalation lever on both sides remained air/missile and maritime — not mobilization.
daily_entries.prediction_impact: The June 27 repeat of the breach-retaliation cycle is the sharpest sign yet that the ceasefire is fragile — but it again ran entirely on the air/maritime rung, leaving Predictive History's imminent-US-ground-invasion and Hormuz-and-Kharg-seizure thesis disconfirmed-and-inverted. Both US responses to Iran's drone attacks were airstrikes on storage, radar and air-defense targets (the same instrument used in the early-June flare-ups), not a landing, a Kharg assault, an ARG/MEU surge, or a draft. The structural inversion holds and hardens: Iran (not the US) is using force to assert coercive control over the Strait — firing on a second tanker, threatening a 'broader response,' menacing Bahrain's airspace — while the US keeps the chokepoint open (JMIC widened the route), the blockade lifted, and Gulf exports climbing to ~75% of pre-war, the opposite of a forcible US seizure of Hormuz and Kharg. The episode meaningfully raises deal-durability risk: this is now a repeating, two-day breach-retaliation cycle, which strengthens the 'fragile ceasefire could re-collapse' reading of the deal-durability open question (iran-us-deal-reached-june-2026) and the 'genuine, hardening sovereignty claim' reading of the Hormuz-governance open question (iran-hormuz-administration-tolls-dispute-june-2026). But a collapse, if it came, would return the war to the air/missile/maritime register — not vindicate a ground invasion.

alternate_readings.reading: The June 27 second strike is read two ways from the same facts. One reading treats the two-day exchange as a contained, proportionate enforcement pattern inside an otherwise-holding 60-day process — each Iranian strike on shipping drawing a discrete, escalating-but-bounded US air response on military targets, with the Strait still open (JMIC even widening the route), the blockade still lifted, oil falling to a four-month low, Gulf exports climbing, and both sides keeping the MOU technically in force while blaming the other. The other reading treats it as a hardening breach-retaliation cycle that is sliding the ceasefire back toward open conflict: a second tanker hit, a US strike explicitly 'larger than last night,' Iran's 'swift and decisive' and 'broader response' warnings, an Iranian drone over Bahrain, Hezbollah declaring the Lebanon framework 'null and void,' and the cycle now repeating day-on-day rather than resolving.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings draw on the same on-record facts (the June 27 M/T Kiku drone strike; the second, larger US airstrike per CENTCOM; the Rezaei and IRGC Navy warnings; the Bahrain sovereignty complaint; the GCC condemnation; the oil move; Hezbollah's rejection; the MOU still nominally in force). Which prevails depends on whether the cycle repeats a third time, whether Iran makes good on its 'broader response' threat, and what the next Geneva technical round produces — not resolvable from open sources today.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 25 (Day 119): With the 60-day Bürgenstock roadmap intact but its two open frictions unresolved, the Strait-of-Hormuz governance question moved alongside the nuclear-inspections dispute as the central fault line. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 23 (Day 117): The first round of US-Iran technical talks at the Bürgenstock resort in Switzerland concluded Monday June 22 with the clearest forward step since the June 17 MOU: mediators Qatar and Pakistan announced the two sides had agreed a 'roadmap toward reaching a final deal within 60 days.' The session — led by VP JD Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, with FM Abbas Araghchi prominent — produced three concrete mechanisms. First, a Lebanon 'deconfliction cell' involving the United States, Iran and Lebanon, facilitated by the mediators, to enforce the cessation of military operations in southern Lebanon; Araghchi called it the framework's '1st real test.' Second, a communications channel to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, defusing the June 20 closure dispute that had shadowed the talks. Third, per Araghchi, a settlement package in which 'oil and petrol exports are waived, blockade lifted, some frozen assets released, and a major reconstruction & development plan launched for Iran.' Technical talks were set to continue through the week at Bürgenstock, with a further round reported for June 23-25 in Washington. Markets read it as de-escalation: Brent slipped about 0.4% to ~$80.26/bbl and WTI traded around $77.52. Lebanon stayed the fragile fault line — fighting continued despite the renewed ceasefire, which is precisely what the new deconfliction cell is meant to stop. The ground rung was unchanged and still de-escalatory on the US side: no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no draft, the naval blockade still lifted, and the USS Boxer amphibious ready group disaggregated. In the other theatres, Kostiantynivka became Russia's principal objective in Donbas while Ukraine extended its Russian-energy strike campaign (Crimea oil terminal June 21, Moscow's Kapotnya refinery June 18); Colombia's Trump-backed president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella prepared to take office August 7; the Maduro/Flores prosecution continued in Manhattan and Cuba's energy emergency deepened; and the US-China trade truce held at ~30% tariffs (paused to Nov 10) even as Washington advanced a proposed 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff. (CNBC; NPR; Al Jazeera; Iran International; CBS News; CNN; ISW, June 21-22, 2026.)

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 22 (Day 116): The week-old war-ending deal came through its most fragile weekend intact but visibly strained, with active diplomacy and escalatory rhetoric running side by side. The in-person US-Iran technical talks that had been postponed Friday did reconvene Sunday June 21 at the Bürgenstock resort in Switzerland — a quadrilateral session (US, Iran, Pakistan, Qatar) led by VP JD Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, with mediators present and an 'emergency session' added on the Lebanon fighting; Vance claimed 'great progress' and framed the aim as turning 'over a new leaf,' but the first ~80-minute session broke for consultations and no final agreement was reported. On the Strait of Hormuz, the United States disputed Iran's June 20 closure claim outright: CENTCOM said 'Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow,' with 55 merchant ships and more than 17 million barrels of oil transiting June 20, and Vance noted Iran had not fired on shipping for a second straight night. Even so, the rhetoric escalated — Trump threatened to 'hit Iran very hard again' and warned Iran 'won't have a country,' while Ghalibaf said Tehran's armed forces are 'ready to respond in another way' — and the Hormuz tolls dispute remained open. The Lebanon ceasefire renewed Friday was repeatedly violated, with roughly 145 killed over two days (cumulative ~4,000 since March 2; more than a million displaced). Oil firmed modestly (WTI ~$79, up ~3% on June 21; Brent ~$80) on the mixed picture. The ground rung stayed unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side — no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, no draft, and the USS Boxer amphibious ready group was disaggregated, a fresh drawdown signal. In the other theatres, Colombia's June 21 presidential runoff was won narrowly by far-right, Trump-endorsed Abelardo de la Espriella over leftist Iván Cepeda (a rightward shift; he takes office August 7), and Ukraine struck a Crimean oil terminal overnight, extending the energy-strike campaign that hit Moscow's Kapotnya refinery on June 18.
details: BÜRGENSTOCK TALKS RECONVENED (June 21, 2026): The postponed in-person US-Iran technical talks went ahead Sunday at the Bürgenstock resort on Lake Lucerne — a quadrilateral session with US (VP JD Vance), Iran (Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf) and mediators Pakistan and Qatar. A first session ran roughly 80 minutes and broke around 15:00 GMT for internal consultations; an 'emergency session' on the Lebanon fighting was added. Vance claimed 'great progress' in the first hours and framed the goal as turning 'over a new leaf.' The talks are technical — implementing the June 17 MOU and opening a nuclear track — and produced no final agreement at search time. (Al Jazeera; CBS News live blog; Wikipedia '2025-2026 Iran-United States negotiations,' June 21, 2026.)

US DISPUTES IRAN'S HORMUZ CLOSURE (June 20-21): CENTCOM rejected Iran's June 20 closure declaration — 'Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow' — and the US said 55 merchant ships carrying more than 17 million barrels of oil transited the strait on Saturday June 20. Vance said Iran had not fired on shipping for a second consecutive night, calling it evidence Tehran is 'honoring their end of the commitment.' The status is thus disputed/effectively-flowing rather than a hard closure, and the US naval blockade itself remains lifted. (CNN live; CBS News live blog, June 20-21, 2026.)

ESCALATORY RHETORIC ALONGSIDE THE TALKS (June 20-21): Even as negotiators met, Trump threatened to 'hit Iran very hard again,' said Iran 'won't have a country,' and (per CBS) vowed to 'blow the [expletive] out of them' if the deal fails; Ghalibaf countered, 'We don't count on the threats of the Americans,' and said Iran's armed forces are 'ready to respond in another way,' warning the US to 'be careful with their statements.' (NPR; CBS News, June 21, 2026.)

HORMUZ TOLLS DISPUTE STAYS OPEN (June 20): On Truth Social, Trump said there will be 'NO tolls after the 60 day period has expired, unless they are imposed by and for the United States of America... for services rendered as the Guardian Angel to the countries of the Middle East' — vowing Iran will not charge Hormuz tolls but signaling the US might. Iran maintains any transit fees are a sovereignty matter, with a Hormuz management regime to be set up with Oman. (Al Jazeera; Fortune; The Hill, June 20, 2026.)

LEBANON CEASEFIRE REPEATEDLY VIOLATED (June 20-21): The US/Qatar/Iran-mediated Israel-Hezbollah truce renewed Friday June 19 did not hold — Israel struck numerous sites in Lebanon, with the death toll rising by roughly 145 over two days; Israel said Hezbollah fired 50+ projectiles (Hezbollah denied). Cumulative Lebanon deaths from Israeli strikes are above 4,000 since March 2, with more than a million displaced; Israeli troops remain in the southern security zone and Netanyahu has refused withdrawal. The Lebanon file was the explicit 'emergency' agenda item at the Swiss talks. (CBS News; PBS News; Wikipedia '2026 Lebanon war,' June 20-21, 2026.)

OIL FIRMS MODESTLY (June 19-21): WTI traded around $78.70/bbl, up roughly 3% on June 21, while Brent's last firm close was $80.57 (June 19); prices fluctuated on the tug between Hormuz re-closure risk and the MOU's de-escalation. Hormuz tanker traffic remained well below the pre-war ~120-130 transits/day — 55 ships moved June 20 (US figure) with an estimated 500+ vessels still waiting to exit the Gulf. Pricing is de-escalation/deal pricing with a residual risk premium, not the sustained $130+ that a US ground commitment would imply. (CBS News live blog; CNBC; Al Jazeera, June 19-21, 2026.)

COLOMBIA SHIFTS FAR-RIGHT (June 21): Colombia's presidential runoff was won narrowly by far-right newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella, who defeated leftist Senator Iván Cepeda (a close Petro ally). Preliminary count (~99.6% tallied): de la Espriella ~49.65% vs. Cepeda ~48.70% — a ~0.95-point margin on the highest turnout since 1998. De la Espriella, endorsed by Trump and Flávio Bolsonaro and running on security, takes office August 7 — a rightward shift in a region the US has been actively reshaping (Venezuela, Cuba). (France 24 live; Wikipedia '2026 Colombian presidential election,' June 21, 2026.)

UKRAINE EXTENDS RUSSIAN-ENERGY STRIKES (June 21): Overnight, Ukraine reportedly struck an oil terminal in occupied Crimea, a follow-on to its June 18 strike on Moscow's Kapotnya (Moscow Oil) refinery — the largest attack on the Russian capital since 2022, which Kyiv framed as retaliation for Russian strikes on the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra. On the ground, Kostiantynivka has become Russia's main objective: Russian forces entered its northeastern part and achieved a tactical breakthrough in the west; formal peace talks remain frozen. (NBC News; NPR; ISW; RBC-Ukraine, June 18-21, 2026.)

OTHER THEATRES: China positioned as Iran-war diplomatic beneficiary — FM Wang Yi spoke with Iran's Araghchi (~June 18-19) urging Hormuz be 'properly handled,' and CNN ran 'China is counting its wins from the Iran war' (June 20). US-China trade holds at ~30% tariffs under a 60-day pause, with a new USTR 12.5% Section 301 tariff proposed. North Korea was quiet in the window (most recent: June 15 modular-launcher / tactical cruise-missile test). Hormuz-affected states kept adapting: Japan expects ~100% non-Hormuz crude in July, India is ~70% non-Hormuz (record Russian-crude imports), Pakistan cut petrol by Rs74/L while co-mediating the Swiss talks, and parts of Europe (Slovenia, Austria) kept rationing/relief measures. Venezuela's Maduro's next Manhattan federal hearing remains set for July 22 (postponed from June 30); Cuba's fuel/energy emergency keeps deepening. (CNN; SCMP; AEI; NK News; Bloomberg; Arab News; Wikipedia, June 2026.)
daily_entries.prediction_impact: June 21-22 leaves Predictive History's imminent-US-ground-invasion and Hormuz-and-Kharg-seizure thesis disconfirmed, and the weekend's events sharpen rather than soften that verdict. The decisive US-side facts cut against the prediction: the talks reconvened (a negotiated, not kinetic, path), CENTCOM publicly disputed Iran's closure and reported traffic still flowing, the naval blockade stays lifted, and the USS Boxer ARG was disaggregated — a fresh drawdown signal, the opposite of an amphibious buildup. What did escalate was rhetoric (Trump's 'hit Iran very hard again') and the air-power/tolls lever, never a ground move. The genuine open question the audit has flagged all along — whether the deal is a durable settlement or another over-sold, fraying announcement — stayed live: the chokepoint the deal was meant to reopen is contested again, the Lebanon ceasefire is being violated, and the toll dispute is unresolved. But none of that is the predicted scenario of US troops taking Hormuz and Kharg by force; the structural inversion (Iran coercing via the strait while the US draws down) holds.

alternate_readings.reading: The actual status of the Strait of Hormuz on June 20-22 is read two ways from the same record. Iran's IRGC declared the strait closed; the United States (CENTCOM) says 'Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow,' citing 55 merchant ships and >17 million barrels transiting June 20. One reading treats the closure as largely declaratory — a coercive Iranian bargaining signal over Israel's Lebanon strikes that has not actually stopped traffic, so the deal's reopening substantively holds. The other treats the US figures as best-case and Iran's declaration plus the still-depressed transit count (a fraction of the pre-war ~120-130/day, with 500+ vessels waiting) as evidence the reopening is fragile and partly reversed.
alternate_readings.evidentiary_status: Both readings rest on documented facts: the IRGC's closure declaration tied to Israel's Lebanon strikes, the CENTCOM 'traffic continues to flow' statement and 55-ship/17M-barrel figure, Vance's 'second night without fire on shipping' claim, and the still-suppressed overall transit volume. Open sources cannot currently reconcile a declared closure with continued (if reduced) flow, nor independently verify the US transit count against Iranian claims.
alternate_readings.public_assertion_by: Iran (IRGC / Speaker Ghalibaf) asserts the closure; the US (CENTCOM, VP Vance) asserts the strait is open and traffic flowing; international shipping and energy press report both alongside reduced transit volumes.
alternate_readings.why_unresolvable: Independent, real-time transit verification through a contested chokepoint is not available in open sources; the closure-vs-flow dispute turns on data each side controls and on intent (declaratory pressure vs. operational closure) that cannot be settled from public reporting in this window.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 22 (Day 116): No change to the ground-invasion picture on the US side, which stayed de-escalatory through the deal's most precarious weekend. The two US-side developments were diplomatic and drawdown-leaning, not ground moves: the postponed in-person US-Iran technical talks reconvened Sunday June 21 at the Bürgenstock resort, and the USS Boxer amphibious ready group / 11th MEU was disaggregated — a fresh de-escalation signal that removes, rather than adds, amphibious mass. CENTCOM publicly disputed Iran's June 20 Hormuz closure ('Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow'), and the US naval blockade itself remains lifted. There are still ~50,000 US troops in the CENTCOM area of responsibility with no new deployment ordered; the USS Tripoli (LHA-7) ARG / 31st MEU (~2,200-2,500 Marines) remains forward-deployed in a routine posture (its blockade-enforcement role wound down); no Kharg assault has been ordered or executed; no third ARG or new MEU has been ordered; and there is no draft signal. The escalation Trump voiced over the weekend ('hit Iran very hard again') is an air-power threat, not a ground deployment. The 82nd Airborne forward headquarters remains a fading standing forcible-entry contingency, not an execution order.
details: TROOP LEVEL: Still ~50,000 US troops in the CENTCOM AOR (official figure, holding since March 2026); no net change and no new ground deployment ordered over the June 21-22 weekend, which was dominated by the Swiss talks and rhetoric, not force movement. (CBS News; Al Jazeera, June 20-21, 2026.)

BOXER ARG DISAGGREGATED — DRAWDOWN SIGNAL (June 20-21): The USS Boxer amphibious ready group / 11th MEU (~4,000 Marines) was disaggregated despite earlier reporting it might join the war — a notable de-escalation data point that removes amphibious mass rather than concentrating it for any landing. (The War Zone; armyrecognition.com, June 2026.)

HORMUZ CLOSURE DISPUTED, BLOCKADE STILL LIFTED (June 20-21): Iran declared the strait closed, but CENTCOM said 'Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow' (55 ships / >17M barrels June 20), and the US naval blockade remains lifted. This is a maritime/diplomatic contest, not a US ground operation. (CNN live; CBS News, June 20-21, 2026.)

KHARG ISLAND: The seizure pathway remains superseded. No US ground troops are on Kharg and no assault has been ordered or executed; the weekend's Hormuz dispute changes the maritime picture but not the ground one. (Al Jazeera; War on the Rocks 'The Folly of Seizing Kharg Island,' April 2026, as standing context.)

MARINE / AMPHIBIOUS — POSTURE TRENDING TO ROTATION/DRAWDOWN: No new amphibious or Marine deployment ordered. The USS Tripoli (LHA-7) ARG / 31st MEU remains forward-deployed in a routine posture (not invasion staging), its enforcement role wound down; the USS Boxer ARG / 11th MEU was disaggregated; the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group was earlier flagged as likely first to rotate out. No third ARG, no new MEU surge, no landing toward Iran or Kharg. (The War Zone; armyrecognition.com, June 2026.)

DRAFT / MOBILIZATION: No draft or conscription signal. The weekend's escalatory rhetoric, the Hormuz dispute and the Lebanon flare-up produced no Selective Service action, no expanded Guard/Reserve call-up language, and no brigade-scale activation. The previously legislated automatic Selective Service registration (effective Dec 2026) is unrelated to the war. (CNN Politics; CNBC, April 9, 2026, as standing context.)

ASSESSMENT: Ground-invasion execution probability is LOW and stable at Day 116. The weekend's stress — the disputed Hormuz status, the violated Lebanon ceasefire, the open toll dispute, and the only-just-reconvened Swiss talks — bears on the deal's durability, not on any US ground move. Every fresh US-side data point (talks reconvening, blockade lifted, Boxer ARG disaggregated) points to de-escalation; the live escalation lever is air-power, not ground.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 21 (Day 115): The war-ending deal survived its first full week but entered its most fragile stretch since the June 17 signing, as Iran reversed the Strait of Hormuz reopening from its own side while the diplomatic track simultaneously moved to reconvene. On June 20 Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps declared the Strait of Hormuz closed again — only two days after commercial transits resumed for the first time in ~110 days — casting Israel's continued strikes on Lebanon as a violation of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding and warning of 'reciprocal action' if Washington does not enforce its commitments. The US naval blockade itself remains lifted (CENTCOM enforcement 'ceased'); the new closure is Iranian leverage, not a return of the US interdiction campaign. Crucially, the talks did not break: Vice President JD Vance departed for the technical US-Iran meeting in Switzerland (the Bürgenstock session postponed on Friday), which Pakistan said was due to reconvene on Sunday June 21 with Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish mediators coordinating — so the process that had stalled appeared to be resuming rather than failing. Iran separately said it was 'ready to move forward' with the deal provided Israel abides by its terms. The Lebanon track, the deal's live fault line, deteriorated: Israeli airstrikes killed at least 32 people in Lebanon on June 20 despite Friday's Trump-brokered Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire renewal, with Al Jazeera reporting the strikes were 'putting US-Iran talks in peril'; MSF said conditions in Nabatieh resembled a 'death trap,' the UK condemned an Israeli minister over 'inflammatory' Lebanon remarks, and the cumulative Lebanon toll since March 2 stood near 4,000 killed. The US announced a new round of Israel-Lebanon talks in Washington the following week. On the tolls dispute, Trump vowed Iran would not be allowed to charge Hormuz tolls but said the US itself might, and reporting indicated the MOU does not rule out future US tolls after an initial 60-day period. The Pentagon told lawmakers it needed roughly $80 billion for the Iran war and other expenses. Oil rose on June 19 on the Lebanon fighting and still-slow Hormuz traffic, with Brent near $80 and WTI near $77, then held in that band — far below wartime peaks above $110. The ground-invasion rung was unchanged and still de-escalatory: Iran's Hormuz re-closure is a coercive maritime move by Tehran, not a US ground operation, and the US posture remained one of drawdown (blockade enforcement ceased, the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group flagged as likely first to rotate out); there are no US troops in Iran, no Kharg assault, and no draft signal. (Al Jazeera live updates; CBS News; The War Zone; oilprice.com; Navy Times, June 19-20, 2026.)

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 20 (Day 114): A day of crosscurrents that left the war-ending deal intact but its diplomatic follow-through stalled. The interim memorandum of understanding signed electronically by Trump and Pezeshkian on June 17 remains in force — the US naval blockade stays lifted and the Strait of Hormuz keeps reopening — but the in-person process to open the 60-day nuclear/sanctions window hit an early snag. Switzerland's foreign ministry confirmed on June 19 that the planned Bürgenstock meeting of the United States, Iran, Qatar and Pakistan 'has been postponed,' giving no new date, after Vice President JD Vance canceled his trip (the White House cited unresolved logistics: 'the logistics of these negotiations have never been simple or predictable') and Iran delayed sending its delegation in protest at Israel's continued operations in Lebanon. CNBC framed it as the accord's first stumble ('hits early snag after Swiss talks fail to proceed as planned'). The Lebanon track — the deal's live fault line — flared sharply: Israeli airstrikes killed at least 16 people in Lebanon overnight and four IDF soldiers were killed in the south, pushing the cumulative toll since March 2 to roughly 4,000 dead, and the escalation threatened to derail the Switzerland talks outright. Trump told NBC News he phoned Israel on Friday afternoon and asked it to agree to a ceasefire; Israel and Hezbollah then agreed to renew their truce, both sides saying they would abide by it while warning against violations. Netanyahu said Israel would respond forcefully to any Hezbollah violation and retain 'complete military freedom of action,' and reiterated Israel will 'not withdraw' from its southern-Lebanon security zone 'as long as Israel's security needs require it.' On the water, Hormuz traffic kept building from a trickle: CENTCOM said 'all U.S. military blockade enforcement efforts have ceased,' sanctioned Iranian tankers entered the strait, and Grimaldi, Cosco and Knutsen vessels moved through, though Lloyd's List estimated ~550 merchant ships still need to exit the Gulf and the central channel stays closed pending clearance of ~80 mines (full normalization 'weeks' away). Brent crude steadied near $80 on Friday — edging up from ~$77 on the talks-postponement uncertainty — but remained on course for a sharp weekly decline. GOP Sen. Roger Wicker said he was 'concerned that the memorandum... negotiates away the victories of Operation Epic Fury.' Vance reiterated that any Iranian Hormuz toll would mean 'there's not going to be a final deal.' The ground-invasion rung was unchanged: the postponement is a diplomatic wobble and the Lebanon flare-up a kinetic air/naval risk, neither a move toward US ground forces; no US troops are in Iran, no Kharg assault has been ordered, and there is no draft signal.

Netanyahu said Israel would respond forcefully to any Hezbollah violation and would retain 'complete military freedom of action,' and repeated that Israel will 'not withdraw' from its southern-Lebanon security zone 'as long as Israel's security needs require it' — defusing, for now, the Iranian-resumption tripwire that had threatened the wider deal while leaving the underlying withdrawal dispute unresolved. (NBC News; CNN live updates, June 19, 2026.)

HORMUZ REOPENING CONTINUES; BLOCKADE ENFORCEMENT 'CEASED' (June 18-19, 2026): US Central Command said 'American forces are not impeding the transit of vessels to or from Iranian ports' and that 'all U.S. military blockade enforcement efforts have ceased'; sanctioned Iranian tankers entered the strait following the announcement, and Grimaldi Group, Cosco and Knutsen vessels were among those transiting. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 19 (Day 113): The June 14 war-ending deal crossed from announcement into consummation. Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the memorandum of understanding electronically Wednesday night — Trump at a candlelit dinner outside Paris during the G7 summit, Pezeshkian remotely — and the agreement took immediate effect, superseding and cancelling the in-person Friday June 19 Geneva ceremony (negotiating teams still gather at the Bürgenstock resort Friday to open a 60-day window on Iran's nuclear program and sanctions relief). US Central Command announced that the naval blockade of Iranian ports has been lifted 'in accordance with the president's direction,' with military vessels remaining only to monitor compliance. Commercial traffic began returning to the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in roughly 110 days: maritime-intelligence firm Windward counted about 18 vessels transiting between the evening of June 17 and midday June 18 (including a French-flagged LNG tanker and Hong Kong-, Italian-, Japanese- and Saudi-linked ships), which its chief analyst called 'a sign of confidence in the agreement'; CBS put Thursday-morning transits at 'at least 10.' This remains a trickle against the ~135 ships/day pre-war norm, routed through the northern (Iranian) and southern (Omani) corridors while the central channel stays closed pending clearance of an estimated 80 mines (CNBC: full normalization will take weeks). VP Vance said '12.5 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz last night,' a war-era high, and warned that any Iranian attempt to 'propose tolls' would mean 'not going to be a final deal' — even as Iran signaled (per Al Jazeera) it will 'charge fees for services' at the strait jointly with Oman, contradicting Trump's toll-free pledge and seeding the next dispute. Brent crude held a three-month-plus low near $77/bbl. Lebanon stayed the unresolved front: the MOU calls for an 'immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,' but Netanyahu declared Israel will 'not withdraw from' its security zone in southern Lebanon, Iran's foreign minister said Israeli forces remaining would violate the agreement, and Hezbollah claimed it repelled Israeli advances Thursday; Lebanon's toll reached ~3,912 killed and 11,873 wounded since March 2 (Israel: 31 soldiers + 1 contractor, one more soldier killed and seven wounded Thursday). The administration briefed congressional leaders Thursday, where GOP Senator Roger Wicker warned the deal 'negotiates away' the military's victories. On the side tracks the G7's June 17 joint Ukraine statement (air-defense pledges, Russia pressure, signed by Trump) and the UK's new 'shadow fleet' sanctions carried forward; in Venezuela the Maduro/Flores Manhattan case's next hearing was confirmed postponed from June 30 to July 22 (World Cup logistics) with Delcy Rodriguez holding the presidency and Cuba's fuel crisis persisting; the US-China trade truce held with Taiwan the flashpoint; and on the Korean Peninsula no new launch followed the June 8-9 Xi-Kim Pyongyang summit.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 18 (Day 112): The June 14 war-ending deal survived the close of the G7 summit, but two unresolved questions — an unreleased text and the Lebanon sticking point — kept the settlement short of consummation. Trump wrapped his final day at the G7 in the French Alps on June 17 with a news conference defending what he branded 'the Trump deal': a 14-point agreement he says includes commitments that Iran 'will never have a nuclear weapon' and that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. He warned that if Iran does not abide by the agreement, the United States 'may restart its bombing campaign' — an air-power threat, not a ground one. G7 allies endorsed the framework (French President Macron called it 'a very good deal'), yet no full MOU text had been released publicly days after a senior US official's 'within 24 to 48 hours' pledge. Officials and reports continue to describe the document as roughly a page and a half — characterized as essentially a commitment to negotiate, opening a second phase of direct talks on Iran's nuclear program, with no stated plan yet to deal with Iran's nuclear capabilities. The in-person signing remained set for Friday June 19 in Switzerland (Bürgenstock/Luzern), with Vice President Vance representing the United States. The Lebanon fault line hardened: Iran's FM Araghchi reiterated that the deal requires Israel to withdraw from Lebanon, a US official says it does not, Netanyahu pledged to remain in 'security zones,' and Israeli ministers said Israel 'won't be bound' by the Iran deal and threatened to strike Hezbollah with 'full force' if attacked. Trump repeated he is 'not happy' with Israel's handling of its 'minor war' in Lebanon. Oil fell a fourth straight session, with Brent near $79/bbl on Wednesday — a three-month low — pressured by expected supply returns once the deal takes effect (Friday signing, higher OPEC+ quotas, additional UAE output after its wartime OPEC exit). Despite the ceasefire, the strait remained closed in practice: ADNOC CEO Sultan Al Jaber said Hormuz is still not open because Iran is restricting and conditioning traffic, with about 230 loaded oil tankers waiting inside the Gulf and transit expected to resume only once the agreement takes effect. On the side tracks, the G7 issued a joint statement pledging renewed support for Ukraine — including strengthened air defense, per Zelensky — and pressure on Russia, which Trump signed onto; the UK unveiled dozens of new sanctions targeting Russia's 'shadow fleet' and sanctions-evasion networks, and the G7 weighed tougher measures on Russia's energy sector.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 16-17 (Day 111): The June 14 war-ending deal held through the opening of the G7 summit, but the Lebanon track hardened into its central unresolved question. At the G7 in Europe on June 16, President Trump hailed the US-Iran memorandum of understanding — 'the oil is plummeting down and the stock market is shooting up like a rocket today' — said the United States 'will not invest money' in Iran (reinforcing the 'no money will exchange hands' line), and a senior US official said the full text of the MOU would be released 'within 24 to 48 hours,' narrowing the prior 'some time after Friday' framing. The in-person signing remained set for Friday June 19 in Switzerland; the Swiss foreign ministry specified the Bürgenstock resort near Luzern (some reports continued to cite Geneva), with each side expected to sign electronically and Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi saying the text was finalized. The day's main new development was a documented dispute over what the unreleased text requires on Lebanon: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the deal requires Israel to withdraw from southern Lebanon ('Without the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territories they occupied during this war, the war has not fully come to an end'), while a US official said the deal 'did not call for an Israeli withdrawal.' Netanyahu (June 15) said Israel would remain in Lebanon 'as long as necessary' and hold 'security zones,' adding 'the struggle is not over'; and Trump, at the G7, voiced open frustration — 'I'm not happy with the way Israel has handled themselves with Lebanon and with Hezbollah,' 'it just goes on forever' — and, asked about a congressional vote on the deal, said 'I like the idea, send it to Congress please.' Markets continued to price de-escalation: Brent fell more than 3% to near $80/bbl on Tuesday June 16 — a fourth straight session of declines and the lowest since early March — after Monday's drop to ~$83.17, with WTI down in tandem. The Strait of Hormuz stayed effectively closed (current traffic ~12-15 ships/day against a pre-war average of 120-140); reopening begins only after Friday's signing, starting with a mine-removal operation by an international naval mission (US, UK, France, Germany) using drone boats and minesweepers, which insurers and shippers estimate at 40-50 days before they transit in volume (the MOU sets removal 'within 30 days'). The Lebanon toll was now put at roughly 4,000 killed, including hundreds of civilians, with more than a million displaced. On the ground-invasion question the day was again decisively de-escalatory: no US ground troops entered Iran, no Kharg assault was ordered or executed, no third ARG and no new MEU were ordered, and no draft action occurred, while the MOU's blockade-lift and force-withdrawal clauses continue to point toward a US drawdown — the structural inverse of Predictive History's imminent-ground-invasion / resource-seizure framing.

The Swiss foreign ministry announced the ceremony would be held at the Bürgenstock resort near Luzern, though several reports continued to refer to Geneva. (PBS NewsHour, June 16, 2026; CBS News live updates, June 16, 2026.)

Because the full MOU text is unreleased, the two readings cannot be reconciled from open sources. (PBS NewsHour, 'Iran says the deal to end the war with the U.S. requires Israel to withdraw from Lebanon,' June 16, 2026; NBC News, June 16, 2026.)

NETANYAHU: ISRAEL STAYS 'AS LONG AS NECESSARY'; TRUMP 'NOT HAPPY,' BACKS CONGRESS REVIEW (June 15-16, 2026): Netanyahu said June 15 that Israel would remain in Lebanon 'as long as necessary,' would hold 'security zones,' and that 'the struggle is not over.' At the G7 on June 16 Trump criticized Israel's handling of its 'minor war' against Hezbollah — 'I'm not happy with the way Israel has handled themselves with Lebanon and with Hezbollah,' 'it just goes on forever' — and, asked about a congressional vote on the Iran deal, said: 'I like the idea, send it to Congress please.' (PBS NewsHour; NBC News; The Times of Israel, June 15-16, 2026.)

OIL EXTENDS SLIDE A FOURTH STRAIGHT SESSION TO NEAR $80 (June 16, 2026): Brent crude fell more than 3% to near $80/bbl on Tuesday — a fourth consecutive session of declines and the lowest since early March — after Monday's 4.7% drop to ~$83.17; WTI fell in tandem, the longest losing streak of the year as the expected Hormuz reopening raised hopes of recovering supply. NBC and others cautioned the relief is being priced ahead of any physical reopening. (CNBC, 'Oil prices: WTI, Brent...'; TradingEconomics; OilPrice.com, June 16, 2026.)

HORMUZ STILL CLOSED; INTERNATIONAL MINE-CLEARING MISSION TO OPEN AFTER FRIDAY (June 16, 2026): The Strait of Hormuz remained effectively closed to commercial traffic — current transits ~12-15 ships/day against a pre-war average of 120-140 — and is to begin reopening only after Friday's signing, starting with mine removal. An international naval mission including the US, Britain, France and Germany plans to clear an estimated 20-plus mines using drone boats, warships and minesweepers; security and shipping firms estimated 40-50 days before insurers, shippers or oil companies are confident enough to transit in volume, against the MOU's 'within 30 days' removal target. The toll underlies the Lebanon-withdrawal dispute and keeps Iran's resumption tripwire live. (PBS NewsHour, June 16, 2026.)

In Latin America, Maduro and co-defendant Cilia Flores' next New York court date stayed set for June 30, Delcy Rodríguez remained acting president of Venezuela, and Cuba's grid/fuel crisis persisted. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 16-17 (Day 111): The ground-invasion rung stayed at no_ground_troops and the day's developments held the posture toward de-escalation. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 15-16 (Day 110): The June 14 war-ending deal held and firmed rather than slipping. On June 15, VP JD Vance disclosed on ABC's 'Good Morning America' that the memorandum of understanding had already been 'digitally' signed on Sunday June 14 by President Trump, Vance, and Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf — narrowing the gap between announcement and consummation that had defined the project's ~39 prior slipped deal timelines, even though the formal in-person ceremony remains set for Friday June 19 in Geneva (to be executed by Vance and Qalibaf) and Trump said the full text would be released 'some time after Friday.' Trump also said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had approved the agreement ('I understand the answer is yes') and that it had been approved 'both in concept and great detail' by the US, Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and others. Iran's Supreme National Security Council confirmed a finalized MOU; per Mehr's 14-point summary the deal provides an immediate and permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts including Lebanon, a complete lifting of the US naval blockade within 30 days, withdrawal of US forces from around Iran, a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, suspension of oil-sales sanctions, a nuclear agreement to be reached within 60 days, and release of roughly $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets during the negotiations. Markets treated it as decisive de-escalation: at Monday's close US WTI fell 4.8% to about $80.75 and Brent fell 4.7% to about $83.17 — both their lowest since the first week of March — while Asian and global equities surged (Japan's Nikkei +5.5%, South Korea's Kospi +5.7%, Taiwan's Taiex +2.7%, US futures higher). Analysts cautioned the relief would be gradual: the strait reopens for mine removal only after Friday's signing, and shipping and insurance figures estimated full normalization could take 'months' (Den Norske Krigsforsikring's Svein Ringbakken) to 'over a year' (shipping executive S.V. Anchan). The deal remained strained by the Lebanon track: Israel's June 14 strikes on Beirut's southern suburbs (Dahieh) killed at least three, and on June 15 Netanyahu said he had 'saved Israel from annihilation,' declined to criticize the US-Iran deal (saying Israel did not yet know its details) but insisted he was 'not limiting' himself in acting to stop Iran's nuclear program or in preserving Israel's 'freedom of operation' against Hezbollah; Israeli ministers said Israel would not consider itself bound by the Iran deal ('if Iran strikes, we'll hit it with full force'); Iran's Qalibaf warned the Israeli Lebanon strikes threatened the agreement; and Trump publicly warned Netanyahu not to 'blow it.' On the ground-invasion question the day was again decisively de-escalatory: no US ground troops entered Iran, no Kharg assault was ordered or executed, no third ARG and no new MEU were ordered, and no draft action occurred, while the MOU's blockade-lift and force-withdrawal clauses point toward an eventual US drawdown — the structural inverse of Predictive History's imminent-ground-invasion / resource-seizure framing.

Iran said the US naval blockade ends 'immediately and completely.' (Al Jazeera, 'US, Iran to sign a peace deal on Friday: What we know,' June 15, 2026.)

OIL EXTENDS PLUNGE TO A THREE-MONTH LOW; GLOBAL EQUITIES SOAR (June 15, 2026): At Monday's close US WTI crude fell 4.8% to about $80.75/bbl and Brent fell 4.7% to about $83.17/bbl — both their lowest since the first week of March (just after the war began Feb 28). Energy broadly tumbled while global stocks rose: Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed about 5.5%, South Korea's Kospi about 5.7%, Taiwan's Taiex 2.7%, Australia's ASX 200 1.5%, with US S&P 500 futures up ~1% and Nasdaq futures up ~1.8%. NBC News noted that whether prices fall much further 'is highly questionable.' Analysts cautioned normalization would be slow: war-risk insurer Svein Ringbakken said even at full capacity restoration to normal 'would take months,' and shipping executive S.V. Anchan predicted 'over a year' for a return to normality. The reopening unwinds the war-risk premium against the EIA's June outlook (which had assumed a still-closed strait keeping Brent near $105 in June-July). (Al Jazeera; NBC News, June 15, 2026.)

Iran's Qalibaf warned the Israeli Lebanon strikes threatened the agreement, and Trump warned Netanyahu not to 'blow it.' (The Times of Israel, June 15, 2026 liveblog; Al Jazeera, June 14, 2026; CNBC, June 14, 2026.)

GROUND RUNG — DE-ESCALATORY (June 15-16, 2026): No US ground troops entered Iran, no Kharg ground assault was ordered or executed, no third ARG and no new MEU were ordered, no BCT-scale Guard activation and no Selective Service/draft action occurred. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 14-15 (Day 109): After 107-plus days of war, the United States and Iran reached a deal to end the conflict. On Sunday June 14, President Trump and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif jointly announced the agreement and Iranian state media broadcast it; Sharif posted that a peace deal 'has been REACHED' and that 'both sides have declared the immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.' Trump wrote on Truth Social that 'The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete' and that he 'hereby fully authorize[s] the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz,' simultaneously authorizing the immediate removal of the US naval blockade ('Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!'). Per US and Iranian accounts the memorandum extends the ceasefire 60 days, reopens Hormuz without tolls (Iran responsible for clearing its own mines, a task that could run into mid-2027), lifts the US blockade and withdraws American forces from the Gulf region, imposes a 15-20 year Iranian enrichment lockout with nuclear-site dismantling, and staggers the release of roughly $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets against compliance — Trump insisting no money changes hands until Iran performs. A formal signing was set for Friday June 19 in Switzerland (reported as Geneva), to be executed electronically by Trump or in person by VP JD Vance. Markets read it as decisive de-escalation: WTI fell more than 4.5% to about $80 and Brent about 4% to roughly $83 as Sunday-evening trading opened — both their lowest since early March. The deal is not yet consummated, however: it remains unsigned until Friday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval was not publicly confirmed, and earlier the same day Iran's Fars/Foreign Ministry had denied that an 'approved text' existed. It is also immediately strained by the Lebanon track: Israel struck a Hezbollah command center in Beirut's Dahieh suburb and killed a senior Hezbollah commander in a 'precise strike' in southern Lebanon around the announcement; Trump said the Beirut attack 'should not have happened... at a time when we are so close to a Peace Deal'; Netanyahu told Trump Israel would not consider itself bound to halt operations in Lebanon; and some oil tankers reportedly paused in the Strait amid the strikes. On the ground-invasion question the day was strongly de-escalatory: the deal would reopen Hormuz by negotiation and withdraw US forces — the structural inverse of Predictive History's imminent-ground-invasion / resource-seizure framing — with no US troops in Iran, no Kharg ground assault, no new ARG/MEU order, and no draft.
details: DEAL REACHED — TRUMP AND PAKISTAN'S SHARIF JOINTLY ANNOUNCE THE END OF THE WAR (June 14, 2026): President Trump and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced Sunday that the US and Iran had reached a deal to end the war, with Iranian state media broadcasting the announcement. Sharif posted on X that a peace deal 'has been REACHED,' adding: 'Both sides have declared the immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.' Trump said the US had achieved 'peace with Iran' and that the deal would 'bring peace and security to the whole region.' (NBC News, 'Deal reached between the United States and Iran, Trump says'; PBS NewsHour; CBS News; Fox News; Axios, June 14, 2026.)

TRUMP AUTHORIZES TOLL-FREE HORMUZ REOPENING AND IMMEDIATE BLOCKADE REMOVAL (June 14, 2026): On Truth Social Trump wrote that 'The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete... I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz,' and authorized 'the immediate removal of the United States Naval blockade,' adding 'Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!' and 'Congratulations to all!' Iran's deputy foreign minister said the memorandum of understanding was complete and that the US naval blockade would end Sunday night. Defense Secretary Hegseth said the reopening would begin 'immediately' but remained contingent on Iranian performance, targeting pre-war shipping volumes within 30 days. (PBS NewsHour; CBS News; Axios; Bloomberg, June 14, 2026.)

REPORTED MOU TERMS (June 14, 2026): Per US and Iranian accounts the deal extends the ceasefire 60 days; reopens the Strait of Hormuz without transit tolls with Iran responsible for clearing its own mines (a task analysts said could extend into mid-2027); suspends the US naval blockade and withdraws American forces from the Gulf region (Iranian state TV left ambiguous whether this covers only war-deployed forces or pre-existing Gulf bases); imposes a roughly 15-20 year Iranian uranium-enrichment lockout with nuclear-site dismantling, some steps immediate on signing and the rest to be negotiated over 60 days; and provides staggered relief of about $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets tied to compliance. Trump emphasized 'no money will exchange hands' until Iran performs. (CBS News; Axios; Al Arabiya; RFE/RL; Bloomberg, June 14, 2026.)

SIGNING SET FOR FRIDAY JUNE 19 IN SWITZERLAND (June 14, 2026): Pakistan's Sharif said a formal signing ceremony was scheduled for Friday in Switzerland (reported as Geneva). Trump told The Wall Street Journal the deal would be signed either by the president electronically or by VP JD Vance in person; Vance said Sunday evening that the logistics were 'still being worked out' but that he planned to attend, with the possibility the president himself could be there. Four US Air Force C-17s had already moved equipment to Europe for Vance's travel. (NBC News; Detroit News/Reuters; Yahoo News, June 12-14, 2026.)

OIL PLUNGES TO A THREE-MONTH LOW (June 14-15, 2026): As trading opened Sunday evening shortly after the announcement, US WTI crude fell more than 4.5% to about $80/bbl — its lowest level since the first week of March — and Brent tumbled roughly 4% to about $83, also its lowest since early March (later trading under ~$87). The move unwound the war-risk premium that had pushed Brent past $100 during the blockade and against the EIA's June outlook, which had assumed a still-closed strait keeping Brent near $105 in June-July. (AOL/Yahoo Finance; CBS News; Bloomberg; EIA June STEO, June 14-15, 2026.)

DEAL UNSIGNED AND ALREADY STRAINED BY A LEBANON STRIKE (June 14, 2026): The agreement is not consummated — it remains unsigned until Friday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval was not publicly confirmed, and earlier on June 14 Iran's IRGC-linked Fars News and Foreign Ministry had said 'no text for a preliminary memorandum of understanding with the United States has been approved.' Hours around the announcement, Israel struck a Hezbollah command center in Beirut's Dahieh suburb and said it killed a senior Hezbollah commander in a 'precise strike' in southern Lebanon. Trump said 'this morning's attack on Beirut should not have happened... at a time when we are so close to a Peace Deal.' Netanyahu told Trump Israel would not consider itself bound to halt operations in Lebanon and refused a Lebanon withdrawal commitment; Iran's parliament speaker warned the strikes could imperil the deal, and some oil tankers reportedly paused in the Strait. (CBS News, 'Iran and U.S. reach deal... as Israeli strikes in Lebanon threaten agreement'; ABC News; Times of Israel, June 14, 2026.)

GROUND RUNG — DE-ESCALATORY (June 14-15, 2026): No US ground troops entered Iran, no Kharg ground assault was ordered or executed, no third ARG and no new MEU were ordered, no BCT-scale Guard activation and no Selective Service/draft action occurred. The only US logistical movement remained the four C-17s carrying signing-ceremony equipment to Europe. The deal's blockade-lift and force-withdrawal clauses point toward an eventual US drawdown from the Gulf — the inverse of a buildup. (NBC News; Axios; PBS NewsHour, June 14, 2026.)
daily_entries.prediction_impact: This is the cleanest disconfirmation yet of Predictive History's imminent-US-ground-invasion / resource-seizure framing for Iran. The reported deal reopens the Strait of Hormuz by negotiation and withdraws US forces from the Gulf rather than seizing the chokepoint or Kharg Island, and Trump has authorized lifting the naval blockade — the structural inverse of the predicted ground buildup, conscription, and oil-field occupation. Together with the absence of any troop movement toward Iran, no Kharg assault, no new amphibious order, and no draft across 109 days, the settlement track strengthens the 'disconfirmed' status of the ground-invasion thesis. The disconfirmation is not yet fully consummated, however: the MOU is unsigned until Friday June 19, Khamenei's approval is unconfirmed, Iran had denied an 'approved text' earlier the same day, and the deal is already strained by an Israeli Beirut strike and Netanyahu's refusal to be bound on Lebanon — any of which could reopen the kinetic track. An actually-signed reopening of Hormuz that holds would be the decisive falsification; a collapse back into strikes would return the question to contested-unresolved rather than vindicate a ground invasion.

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 13-14 (Day 108): The war reached its scheduled signing day with the agreement still unratified by Tehran. On Saturday June 13, Trump posted on Truth Social that the deal was 'scheduled to get signed tomorrow, and immediately after it is signed, the Hormuz Strait is OPEN TO ALL,' framing the pact as a guarantee of 'long-term peace in the region.' He cast it as the inverse of the 2015 JCPOA — 'A WALL TO NO NUCLEAR WEAPON,' with Iran that 'no longer want[s] a Nuclear Weapon, nor will they have one' — and introduced two new wrinkles: that 'no money will exchange hands' (cutting against the reported $24 billion frozen-assets release that Iran had made a precondition), and that the United States 'will go in and get the Nuclear Dust, buried deep under the powerful sunken granite mountains' at an undetermined later time 'when all is calm,' to be down-blended and destroyed. The signing was set for Europe — reported as Geneva — with Vice President JD Vance and negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attending and Trump himself not attending; four US Air Force C-17 transport planes had departed to Europe on Thursday to move equipment for Vance's possible travel to the ceremony. But caution ran through the day: a senior administration official said Friday the US was not '100%' confident the agreement would be signed; Iran's Foreign Ministry said Tehran had 'not yet reached a final decision'; and as of midweek Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval had not been confirmed even as lower-level Iranian officials signed off — against a backdrop in which Trump had described a deal as imminent roughly 39 times. Oil held near its lowest level in nearly two months (Brent in the high-$80s) on signing optimism, with the US energy secretary saying Strait of Hormuz ship traffic was increasing. In Lebanon, the cumulative toll since March 2 stood near ~3,700 killed as Israeli strikes on Tyre and the south continued under the standing full-city evacuation order, keeping Iran's resumption tripwire live. The other theatres were static: Russia-Ukraine fighting concentrated around Pokrovsk (no operational Russian advance west of the city since December 2025) with the next Istanbul round set for June 20-30; Maduro and Cilia Flores hold a June 30 New York court date with Delcy Rodriguez still president in Caracas amid Cuba's grid/fuel crisis; the US-China trade truce held; and the Xi-Kim Pyongyang summit's 'strategic cooperation' pledge stood. On the ground-invasion question the day stayed de-escalatory: the only US logistical movement was C-17s carrying equipment to Europe for the signing ceremony — not a combat deployment toward Iran — and every EXECUTION indicator stayed at zero (no US ground troops in Iran, no Kharg ground assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no Guard activation, no draft). The one ground-relevant nuance was Trump's restated intent to eventually send personnel 'in' to retrieve nuclear material, but only at an undetermined post-deal time 'when all is calm.' (Bloomberg; CNBC; Fox News; Times of Israel; Just The News; NBC News, June 13, 2026.)

daily_entries.summary: JUNE 13-14 (Day 108): The ground-invasion EXECUTION rung stayed at zero on the war's scheduled signing day, and the dominant vector remained a negotiated end. The one ground-relevant nuance was Trump's restated intent that the US 'will go in and get the Nuclear Dust' — a possible future in-country retrieval of nuclear material — but explicitly deferred to an undetermined time 'when all is calm,' i.e., a post-deal, presumably consented step rather than a forcible-entry order. daily_entries.summary: JUNE 12-13 (Day 107): The war reached its closest approach yet to a negotiated end while remaining unsigned and visibly contested. A day after Trump announced 'a great settlement of the war with Iran,' Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Islamabad's mediators believed a 'final, agreed upon text' had been reached and were working with both sides to finalize next steps, adding that peace 'has never been this close as it is now.' US officials said Iran was holding 'final' deliberations and that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was 'comfortable' with the negotiations and had committed that Iran would 'never procure or develop nuclear weapons.' Trump said a signing could come 'maybe over the weekend in Europe,' with Vice President JD Vance attending, and the UK was reported set to host a meeting of about 35 countries to coordinate reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The reported 14-point MOU tracks the long-discussed framework: Hormuz reopened without tolls and a return to pre-war shipping volumes within 30 days, the US lifting its naval blockade and withdrawing forces from areas around Iran, a suspension of sanctions, the release of $24 billion in frozen Iranian funds, and Iran removing and destroying its nuclear material and dismantling its weapons program. But the agreement was not signed, and the day laid bare a public dispute over its contents: Trump denied Iran's account, posting that leaked terms 'have NOTHING to do' with what had been agreed and branding the Iranians 'very dishonorable people to deal with,' while Iran's Mehr news agency said final negotiations would not begin until half of the $24 billion was released and the US naval blockade ended. Netanyahu's office reiterated that Israel is not a party to the memorandum. The war also stayed kinetic even as the deal advanced: overnight June 11-12 Iranian drones fired on Indian commercial shipping departing the Strait of Hormuz, and US forces shot down two Iranian attack drones near the strait early June 12; Trump called the attack on the Indian ships 'totally unacceptable.' Markets read the trajectory as de-escalation: Brent crude extended its slide toward ~$88.40-$88.65/bbl — its lowest level in nearly two months — and the US pump average eased to about $4.11/gal. In Lebanon, the cumulative toll since March 2 stood near ~3,700 killed (Israeli losses 29 soldiers + 1 civilian contractor) as Christian religious leaders from Tyre appealed to the international community to prevent an Israeli assault on the city's Christian district under the standing full-city evacuation order; Hezbollah's rejection of last week's conditional truce kept Iran's resumption tripwire live. The other theatres were static: Russia-Ukraine fighting concentrated around Pokrovsk (no operational Russian advance west of the city since December 2025) with the next Istanbul round set for June 20-30; Maduro and Cilia Flores hold a June 30 New York court date with Delcy Rodriguez still president in Caracas amid Cuba's grid/fuel crisis; the US-China trade truce held; and the Xi-Kim Pyongyang summit's 'strategic cooperation' pledge stood. On the ground-invasion question the day was de-escalatory: the June 11 Kharg-seizure threat went unacted-upon as the deal route dominated, and every EXECUTION indicator stayed at zero — no US ground troops in Iran, no Kharg ground assault, no new ARG/MEU order, no Guard activation, no draft.

STILL NO US GROUND TROOPS IN IRAN, NO KHARG ASSAULT, NO THIRD-ARG ORDER, NO NEW MEU ORDER, NO BCT-SCALE GUARD ACTIVATION, NO SELECTIVE SERVICE/DRAFT ACTION.
daily_entries.summary: Ground-invasion EXECUTION rung UNCHANGED at Day 107, and the day cut de-escalatory. The June 11 Kharg-seizure / 'total control' threat went unacted-upon: rather than staging a landing, the US spent June 12 advancing a negotiated settlement whose reported 14-point terms would WITHDRAW US forces from areas surrounding Iran, lift the naval blockade, and reopen Hormuz by agreement — the inverse of a ground-commitment posture. No tracked EXECUTION indicator moved: no US or allied ground force entered Iran, no Kharg ground assault was ordered or executed, no third ARG order, no new MEU order, no BCT-scale National Guard activation, and no Selective Service/draft action. A fresh overnight Iranian drone attack on Indian shipping in the Strait drew a US air/naval response (two drones downed), not a ground move. Standing capability is unchanged: ~50,000 US troops in CENTCOM; three carrier strike groups plus the USS Tripoli ARG / 31st MEU enforcing the blockade; USS Boxer ARG / 11th MEU still under INDOPACOM; the 82nd Airborne forward HQ (Maj Gen Tegtmeier) remains a standing Kharg forcible-entry CONTINGENCY, not an execution order. Note: if signed, the MOU's force-withdrawal and blockade-lift clauses would point toward an eventual drawdown, not a buildup.
details: NO MOVE ONTO THE GROUND RUNG (June 12-13, 2026): The June 11 Kharg-seizure threat was not executed; June 12 was dominated by the deal track (Pakistan's 'final text,' a weekend-signing timeline, Khamenei reportedly 'comfortable'). No US ground troops entered Iran, no amphibious or airborne assault was ordered or executed, no Kharg landing occurred. The overnight Iranian drone attack on Indian Hormuz shipping was answered with a US air/naval intercept (two drones downed), not a ground action.

DEAL TERMS POINT AWAY FROM A GROUND BUILDUP (June 12, 2026): The reported 14-point MOU would WITHDRAW US forces from areas surrounding Iran, LIFT the naval blockade, and reopen Hormuz without tolls within 30 days — structurally the opposite of a ground-invasion or resource-seizure trajectory. The unresolved sequencing dispute (Iran wants half the $24B released and the blockade ended before final talks; Trump denies Iran's account) keeps the deal contested, but neither side's position involves a US ground deployment.

STANDING CAPABILITY UNCHANGED (June 12-13, 2026): ~50,000 US troops in the CENTCOM AOR (holding since March 2026); three carrier strike groups; the USS Tripoli ARG + embarked 31st MEU (~2,200 Marines, F-35Bs) on station enforcing the Hormuz blockade and ground-capable if ordered; USS Boxer ARG + 11th MEU (~5,000 Marines) still under INDOPACOM with no redeployment order; the 82nd Airborne forward HQ (Maj Gen Tegtmeier) remains a standing Kharg forcible-entry CONTINGENCY capability, not an execution order. No third ARG ordered, no new MEU order, no BCT-scale Guard activation.

NO DRAFT / CONSCRIPTION SIGNAL (June 12-13, 2026): The day's deal advance and the drone incident produced no Selective Service action, no expanded Guard/Reserve call-up language, and no BCT-scale activation. The only standing item remains the pre-existing administrative plan for automatic Selective Service registration of men 18-26 by end-2026 (CNBC, Apr 9, 2026) — not a draft activation; fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Poynter) continue to rate reinstatement claims false. The House's June 3 war-powers resolution (215-208) remains the dominant counter-mobilization domestic signal.
